entry.title: SAP Joule in SAP S4HANA Cloud Private Edition Navigation, Transactions & Fiori Launchpad
entry.content:
SAP Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Navigation, Transactions & Fiori Launchpad Plug-In Configuration

Introduction

SAP Joule is SAP's generative AI copilot, deeply embedded within the SAP ecosystem to transform how users interact with enterprise applications. Rather than navigating complex menus or memorizing transaction codes, users can express their intent in natural language and let Joule guide them — whether that means navigating to the right SAP Fiori app, executing a transaction, retrieving information, or generating analytical insights. 

Joule is available for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (2021 onwards), SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, SAP SuccessFactors, and SAP Build Code, and is unlocked through product licensing that includes Joule messages. 

Three SAP Notes are particularly important for anyone implementing or operating Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: 3751657, 3523238, and 3799821. Together, they address the activation, capabilities, and consulting boundaries of Joule — forming a practical reference triad for administrators, consultants, and power users alike.

SAP Note 3751657 – How to Configure and Activate Joule Plug-In in a Target Mapping (SAP Fiori Launchpad)

What it addresses: One of the most common early hurdles when deploying Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition is making the Joule icon visible and accessible within the SAP Fiori Launchpad. SAP Note 3751657 directly addresses this challenge. 

Core guidance: To enable the Joule icon in the Fiori Launchpad of an S/4HANA Private Cloud system, the Joule Plug-In must be configured in a target mapping within the SAP Fiori Launchpad. The note provides step-by-step guidance (via an attached document) covering: 

  • Creating a Technical Catalog in the Launchpad App Manager using transaction /n/UI2/FLP
  • Configuring a target mapping with the intent Shell-plugin
  • Creating a new Role in Role Maintenance (/npfcg) and assigning the catalog to it
  • Assigning the JOULE_ADMIN technical user created during prerequisites 

Joule-specific impact: Without this configuration, the Joule icon simply does not appear in the Fiori Launchpad — meaning users have no entry point to the AI copilot, regardless of whether all other BTP-side configurations are correctly in place. This note is therefore a critical activation step in the end-to-end Joule setup journey. 

 

SAP Note 3523238 – Navigational and Transactional Capabilities with Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition

What it addresses: Once Joule is activated, the natural next question is: what can it do? SAP Note 3523238 is the definitive reference for understanding the full scope of Joule's capabilities in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. 

Core guidance: The note outlines two primary capability types:

  • Navigational Capabilities: Joule navigates users to the relevant SAP Fiori app based on a natural language prompt. This is especially valuable for new or occasional users unfamiliar with individual app names. Supported areas include Procurement, Finance, Sales, Service Management, Production Planning, Extended Warehouse Management, and Resource Scheduling. Example prompts include "Which app should I use to clear a GL account?" or "Where can I manage warehouse tasks?" 
  • Transactional Capabilities: Users can carry out tasks directly within Joule — without opening the relevant SAP Fiori app. Supported areas include Finance, Sales, Procurement, Manufacturing, Asset Management, R&D Engineering, and Cross-area functions. Activation of the relevant OData services is a mandatory prerequisite for each transactional use case. 

The note also references two key attachments:

  • Joule for SAP S4HANA Cloud Private Edition Navigational Capabilities.xlsx — a detailed list of all Fiori apps enabled for Joule navigation
  • Business Roles and API for Transactional Capabilities.xlsx — the associated business roles and OData services required per transactional use case 

For issues related to Joule capabilities, the note directs users to raise tickets under component CA-FLP-EXT-PCE-JOULE, and references SAP Note 3746234 (Role and OData Analyser) for verifying custom roles and OData activation status. 

Joule-specific impact: This note is the single most important reference for Joule capability planning. It enables administrators and consultants to map business requirements to specific Joule features, identify the exact OData services to activate, and assign the correct business roles to users — all of which are prerequisites for Joule to deliver transactional and navigational responses rather than falling back to generic informational replies. 

SAP Note 3799821 – Consulting Topics for Joule

Note: SAP Note 3799821 was not directly available in the verified sources reviewed. The closest matching SAP Note covering consulting scope, boundaries, and support classification for Joule is SAP Note 3704471 – Consulting Topics for Joule . The content below is based on that note. If SAP Note 3799821 covers a different specific topic, please verify its content directly on SAP for Me (me.sap.com).

What it addresses: Not every Joule issue is a support issue — and understanding this distinction saves significant time during implementation. SAP Note 3704471 (aligned with the consulting topics theme) clarifies which Joule-related issues fall under SAP Technical Support versus Consulting. 

Core guidance: The note establishes that many Joule issues stem from faulty or insufficient integration with other SAP products, rather than product defects. Key classifications include: 

  • Out of scope for Technical Support: Joule end-to-end initial configuration, licensing and entitlement questions, "how-to" questions, and customer-specific setup scenarios (e.g., configuring Joule without a shared Cloud Identity Service tenant or Global User ID)
  • In scope for Technical Support: Processing errors, "Digital Assistant not Found" messages, Internal Server Errors, and issues preventing Joule from functioning at all
  • Configuration-related issues (e.g., Joule returning generic informational responses instead of navigational/transactional results) are classified as Consulting, as they typically indicate an integration misconfiguration 

Consulting options available:

  • Cloud Readiness Service — validates that all prerequisites and configurations for Joule are correctly in place
  • AI Factory — provides guidance on setting up Joule
  • Expertise on Demand / SAP Consulting — for deeper engagement via your SAP Account Manager 

Joule-specific impact: This note helps teams set realistic expectations before raising support tickets and directs them to the right channel — whether self-service resources, consulting engagements, or technical support — based on the nature of their issue. 

Key Takeaways for SAP Joule Users

  • Activation is a multi-step process: Enabling Joule in the Fiori Launchpad requires explicit plug-in configuration in a target mapping (SAP Note 3751657). Do not assume Joule will appear automatically after BTP-side setup. 
  • Capabilities are role- and OData-dependent: Joule's transactional and navigational features only work when the correct business roles are assigned to users and the required OData services are activated in the back end. SAP Note 3523238 is your go-to reference for this mapping. 
  • Know the support boundary: Configuration issues are Consulting, not Support. If Joule is returning generic informational responses instead of executing navigational or transactional tasks, the root cause is almost always an integration or configuration gap — not a product defect. Use the Cloud Readiness Service or AI Factory for these scenarios. 
  • Joule respects your authorization model: Through Principal Propagation, Joule operates strictly within existing SAP S/4HANA authorization boundaries. Users can only access data and perform actions for which they already hold authorization. 
  • Release version matters: Not all Joule capabilities are available from release 2021. Higher releases unlock additional functionality. Always verify capability availability against your specific S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition release. 

Conclusion

SAP Joule represents a fundamental shift in how users interact with SAP S/4HANA — moving from menu-driven navigation to natural language conversation. However, realizing this potential requires careful attention to activation, capability configuration, and support boundaries.

SAP Notes 3751657, 3523238, and the consulting guidance note together form a practical implementation framework: activate Joule correctly in the Fiori Launchpad, configure the right roles and OData services for your desired capabilities, and understand where to turn when issues arise. With these foundations in place, organizations can unlock Joule's full potential — from navigating users to the right app in seconds, to executing transactions through conversation, to delivering analytical insights on demand.    

For the latest capability updates, always refer to the What's New for Joule documentation on SAP Help Portal, which is continuously updated with new use cases across S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, Public Edition and beyond. 

Refer to:

What's New for Joule | SAP Help Portal

3721491 - Clarifications and Constraints on Integrating S4 HANA Cloud, Private Edition with Joule - SAP for Me

3523238 - Navigational and Transactional capabilities with Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition - SAP for Me (Consider Attachments).

3751657 - How to configure and activate Joule Plug-In in a target mapping (SAP Fiori Launchpad) - SAP for Me (Consider Attachments).

Hope this helps you!

Thank you and regards.

Rogerio Lima.

entry.title: SAP EWM Returnable Packaging Material GR 501 M Using BADI
entry.content:
Introduction

In many manufacturing and consumer goods industries, suppliers deliver materials using reusable packaging such as plastic totes, pallets, crates, containers, and reusable bins. While the purchased raw materials become company inventory through the normal procurement process, the packaging itself often remains vendor-owned and must be tracked separately.

During a recent SAP S/4HANA and SAP EWM implementation, we encountered a requirement to automatically create inventory postings for returnable packaging materials during Goods Receipt without requiring additional manual transactions by warehouse users.

This blog explains how we designed a solution using a BADI enhancement that automatically creates a returnable packaging item and posts it through Movement Type 501M during the inbound process. The approach eliminates manual posting activities and improves inventory accuracy. The overall business scenario is consistent with SAP returnable packaging processing and automatic generation of packaging-related delivery items documented in SAP resources.

 

Business Requirement

The business received raw materials from suppliers in reusable packaging.

Example

Material

Quantity

Raw Material A

100 KG

Plastic Tote

5 EA

Business expected:

  • Raw Material A should post through standard movement type 101.
  • Plastic Totes should post separately using 501M.
  • Warehouse operators should perform only one Goods Receipt transaction.
  • No manual MIGO entries should be required after receipt.

Without automation, operators had to:

  1. Post Goods Receipt for material (101)
  2. Execute separate posting for packaging (501M)
  3. Enter packaging quantities manually

This created:

  • Additional workload
  • Inventory discrepancies
  • Audit concerns
  • User errors

 

System Landscape

The implemented landscape consisted of:

  • SAP S/4HANA
  • SAP EWM Embedded
  • Inbound Delivery Processing
  • Advanced Shipping and Receiving Integration

Goods movements were executed in EWM and replicated to S/4HANA.

 

Solution Design

The solution automatically creates an additional inbound delivery item representing the returnable packaging material.

When Goods Receipt is posted:

Main Product

1     Movement Type = 101

2     Stock Type     = Company Owned

Packaging Material

1     Movement Type = 501M

2     Special Stock = M

3     Stock Type    = Vendor-Owned Returnable Packaging

The process generates a single inventory posting while maintaining separate inventory ownership.

 

Process Flow

1     Purchase Order Created

2              │

3              ▼

4     Inbound Delivery Replicated to EWM

5              │

6              ▼

7                   Packaging

8              │

9              ▼

10             Goods Receipt

11             │

12             ▼

13     Additional Delivery Item Created

14             │

15             ▼

16     Warehouse Processing

17             │

18             ▼

19     Goods Receipt Posted

20             │

21             ├── Material Item → 101

22             │

23             └── Packaging Item → 501M

24             │

25             ▼

26     Material Document Created in S/4HANA

 

Technical Design

Packaging Material Determination

The first challenge was identifying which packaging material should be posted.

The determination logic used:

  • Vendor
  • Material
  • Packaging Type
  • Quantity Conversion
  • Handling Unit Information

Example:

1     1 Tote = 20 KG Material

2    

3     Received Quantity = 100 KG

4    

5     Packaging Quantity = 100 / 20

6    

7     Result = 5 Totes

 

BAdI Enhancement

Use BAdI - /SCWM/EX_DLV_GM_STOCK_ATTR implementation was developed to:

  1. Use Method - GET_STOCK_USAGE
  2. Read Item Category = PAC
  3. Set Stock Usage = ‘E’
  4. Use Method - GET_STOCK_OWNER
  5. Get Vendor Number and Pass Owner = Vendor No

The enhancement was executed automatically during inbound delivery processing, ensuring that users were not required to enter packaging details manually.

 

Material Master Configuration

The packaging material required:

Material Type

1     LEIH

or company-specific packaging material type.

Key Settings

  • Inventory Managed
  • Quantity Updated
  • Warehouse Managed
  • Returnable Packaging Relevant

Proper material master configuration was necessary for successful posting. During initial testing, missing packaging settings prevented automatic packaging item creation.

 

Movement Type Configuration

Movement Type used:

1     501M

Purpose:

1     Goods Receipt without reference

2     Vendor-owned returnable stock

Inventory Impact:

1     Vendor-Owned Stock Increase

Financial Impact:

1     Configured via OBYC account determination

The movement type determination logic required alignment with Returnable Packaging configuration and special stock indicator M.

 

Testing Challenges Encountered

Challenge 1: Packaging Item added w/o Stock Usage = E

Issue

Additional delivery item generated but Stock Usage = Blank

Root Cause

No Standard Solution

Resolution

BADI - /SCWM/EX_DLV_GM_STOCK_ATTR=>GET_STOCK_USAGE need to implement

 

Challenge 2: Packaging Item added Owner = Warehouse Owner

Issue

Additional delivery item generated but Owner = Warehouse Owner

Root Cause

No Standard Solution

Resolution

BADI - /SCWM/EX_DLV_GM_STOCK_ATTR=> GET_STOCK_OWNER

 

Business Benefits

After implementation:

Reduced Manual Effort

Warehouse users perform only one Goods Receipt transaction.

Improved Inventory Accuracy

Returnable packaging stocks are automatically tracked.

Better Audit Compliance

Every packaging receipt is documented through system-generated postings.

Real-Time Visibility

Inventory teams can monitor:

  • Returnable pallets
  • Reusable containers
  • Plastic totes
  • Packaging losses

Reduced Operational Errors

Automation eliminates manual postings after Goods Receipt.

 

Example Material Document

1     Material A

2     Movement Type: 101

3     Quantity: 100 KG

4    

5     Plastic Tote

6     Movement Type: 501M

7     Quantity: 5 EA

Single Goods Receipt transaction generates both postings automatically.

 

Lessons Learned

  1. Validate packaging material master settings early.
  2. Test quantity conversion thoroughly.
  3. Ensure movement type determination is aligned with business ownership rules.
  4. Include exception handling when packaging quantities cannot be calculated.
  5. Perform integration testing between EWM and S/4HANA before user acceptance testing.

 

Conclusion

Managing returnable packaging is a common challenge in warehouse operations, especially when suppliers use reusable containers and pallets. Standard Goods Receipt processing often requires additional manual postings to maintain packaging inventory, increasing operational effort and the risk of discrepancies.

By implementing a BAdI enhancement in SAP EWM, we updated Stock Usage = E and Owner = Vendor No for returnable packaging items and enabled posting through Movement Type 501M during Goods Receipt. The solution improved inventory visibility, reduced manual effort, and ensured accurate tracking of vendor-owned packaging materials while preserving a simple Goods Receipt experience for warehouse users.

This approach demonstrates how targeted SAP EWM enhancements can address real business challenges while maintaining a highly automated warehouse execution process.

The introduction of automated returnable packaging processing into SAP EWM greatly simplified warehouse operations as part of our project. We achieved this by improving the BADI /SCWM/EX_DLV_GM_STOCK_ATTR function, which allowed the correct stock usage and vendor ownership attributes to be automatically assigned for packaging materials and made sure that returnable packaging which was owned by a vendor was posted using Movement Type 501M during the same Goods Receipt procedure as the purchased material.

In terms of its operational function, warehouse users did not have to carry out individual inventory postings or carry out any further transactions following Goods Receipt. This cut down on the amount of manual work, avoided the usual kinds of data entry errors, and increased the accuracy with which returnable packaging inventory could be tracked. Tests of the integration proved that the solution functioned reliably throughout inbound delivery processing, during the execution of EWM Goods Receipt and in S/4HANA inventory postings, all while keeping a clear distinction between company-owned stock and vendor-owned packaging assets.

A key lesson learned during the implementation was that success is determined not just by enhancement logic but also by the correct setup of the material master and the returnable packaging configuration. When implementing this solution once more, we would check the packaging master data and stock ownership requirements much earlier in the project lifecycle to decrease the number of testing iterations.

In summary, the solution showed that a modest enhancement to SAP EWM can produce tangible operational benefits by automating a process which is usually carried out manually and at the same time offering better visibility and control over vendor-owned returnable packaging materials.

entry.title: SAP EWM Planned Replenishment: Storage Type Level vs Fixed Bin Level
entry.content:
Replenishment keeps picking or production-supply areas stocked by moving inventory from reserve storage. In SAP Extended Warehouse Management, the process calculates a requirement, determines suitable source stock, creates an internal warehouse task, groups that task into a warehouse order, and records the physical movement when the task is confirmed.

 

Replenishment methods

Abstract:

Planned replenishment in SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) supports the controlled movement of stock from reserve storage to picking areas so that sufficient inventory is available for order fulfillment.

This article focuses exclusively on planned replenishment - It explains the common configuration and compares two approaches for maintaining minimum and maximum quantities: at storage-type level and at fixed-bin level.

 Storage-type-level planning reduces master-data maintenance but provides less granular control, while fixed-bin-level planning allows replenishment quantities to reflect the requirement of each dedicated picking bin.

The choice depends on warehouse layout, product velocity, bin assignment, and the required level of stock control.

In below storage types, LRRS would be source storage type and LRRH is replenish storage type.

Common Customization: These customizations required for both types of replenishment – Storage type & Fixed Bin

#1 Define storage type

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-MASTER DATA-STORAGE TYPE

Two storage types are used in this replenishment scenario. Storage type LRRS represents the offsite slow-moving or reserve storage area and acts as the source for replenishment. Storage type LRRH represents the onsite fast-moving picking area and acts as the destination. When stock in LRRH falls below the maintained minimum quantity, SAP EWM creates a replenishment warehouse task to move the required quantity from LRRS to LRRH.

#2 Define Activity area

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-MASTER DATA-ACTIVITY AREAS-DEFINE ACTIVITY AREA

Activity areas are created for both storage types to organize warehouse activities and support warehouse-task sorting and warehouse-order creation. Activity area LRRS is defined for the offsite reserve storage type, while activity area LRRH is defined for the onsite fast-moving storage type. In the next configuration steps, the relevant storage bins are assigned to these activity areas and arranged using the required sort sequence.

#3 Assign Storage bin to Activity area

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-MASTER DATA-ACTIVITY AREAS-ASSIGN STORAGE BIN TO ACTIVITY AREA

In this step, the storage bins from storage types LRRS and LRRH are assigned to their respective activity areas. Sequence number 1 defines the order in which SAP EWM considers the assignments. This configuration connects the physical storage bins with the relevant activity area and supports task sorting, queue determination, and warehouse-order creation during replenishment execution.

#4 Define sort sequence of bins to Activity area

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-MASTER DATA-ACTIVITY AREAS-DEFINE SORT SEQUENCE OF BINS TO ACTIVITY AREA

The storage-bin sort sequence is maintained for each relevant warehouse activity within activity areas LRRH and LRRS. The activities include putaway, picking, replenishment, internal movement, and posting changes. For the planned replenishment process, activity REPL is particularly relevant.

This configuration determines the sequence in which storage bins are presented and processed during warehouse-task and warehouse-order execution. A suitable sort sequence reduces unnecessary travel and helps warehouse operators execute replenishment tasks efficiently. In this scenario, sequence number 1 is assigned to the applicable activities for both storage types.

#5 Activate replenishment strategies in Storage type

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-INTERNAL WH PROCESS - REPLENISHMENT CONTROL-ACTIVATE THE REPLENISHMENT STYRATEGIES

Planned replenishment is activated for destination storage type LRRH by assigning replenishment strategy 1 – Planned Replenishment. This setting makes the storage type relevant for planned replenishment processing.

During the replenishment run, SAP EWM checks the available stock in LRRH against the maintained minimum and maximum quantities. When the available stock falls below the minimum level, the system calculates the required replenishment quantity and creates warehouse tasks to move stock from the reserve storage area to LRRH.

The replenishment strategy is activated only for the destination storage type. Source storage type LRRS supplies the stock and does not require the planned-replenishment strategy.

#6 Maintain Doc type and Item type against Warehouse process type

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-INTERNAL WH PROCESS - REPLENISHMENT CONTROL-MAINTAIN DOC TYPE ITEM TYPE

Warehouse process type 3010 – Replenishment is assigned document type SRPL and item type SRPL. This mapping controls the document structure used when SAP EWM creates an internal warehouse request for replenishment.

During the planned replenishment run, the system uses this configuration to create the replenishment warehouse request and its corresponding item. Warehouse tasks are then generated with warehouse process type 3010 to move stock from the reserve storage type to the replenishment-relevant picking area.

The assigned document type, item type, and warehouse process type must be compatible; otherwise, the system may calculate a replenishment requirement but fail to create the warehouse request or warehouse task.

#7 Specify the storage type search sequence

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-GOODS ISSUE PROCESS - STRATEGIES-SPECIFY THE STORAGE TYPE SEARCH SEQUENCE

Storage type search sequence REPL is defined to determine the source storage types used during replenishment. In this scenario, reserve storage type LRRS is assigned as sequence number 1, which means SAP EWM searches this storage type first when selecting stock for replenishment.

When the system creates a replenishment warehouse task for destination storage type LRRH, it uses search sequence REPL to identify the source storage type. The actual source bin and stock are then selected based on the applicable stock-removal strategy and available stock.

Additional reserve storage types can be included in the sequence when required. Their sequence numbers determine the order in which SAP EWM searches them.

#8 Determine the storage type search sequence

SPRO-SCM EWM-EWM-GOODS ISSUE PROCESS - STRATEGIES-DETERMINE THE STORAGE TYPE SEARCH SEQUENCE

In this configuration, warehouse process type 3010 – Replenishment is assigned storage type search sequence REPL. This assignment tells SAP EWM which storage types should be searched when stock is removed to fulfill a replenishment requirement.

The stock-removal rule FIFO is also assigned. Therefore, after search sequence REPL identifies reserve storage type LRRS, SAP EWM gives priority to the stock with the earliest goods receipt date, subject to stock eligibility and other removal criteria.

This configuration connects the replenishment warehouse process type with the source storage type search and stock-removal logic. Without this determination, SAP EWM may calculate the replenishment requirement but fail to identify suitable source stock for warehouse-task creation.

a)Storage Type Level: During the planned replenishment run, the system considers the total stock across all relevant bins within the storage type when calculating the replenishment requirement.

Best case use:

  • Bulk Storage Areas– Ideal for storage types where bins are interchangeable (e.g., block storage, pallet racks).
  • High-Volume, Fast-Moving Items– Useful when exact bin-level tracking is not required and stock is frequently redistributed.
  • Simplified Replenishment Control– Reduces maintenance effort since you define thresholds once per storage type rather than per bin.

 Limitations:

  • Less Granular Control– Replenishment is based on total stock in the storage type, which may not reflect actual bin-level shortages.

Risk of Overstocking/Stockouts - Because the planned run evaluates stock at storage-type level, an individual bin may be empty even when the total stock is sufficient, and replenishment may not be proposed for that bin.

Specific Configuration: Storage type “LRRH”

The Repl. Level field determines the level at which SAP EWM calculates the replenishment requirement. When this field is blank, replenishment is calculated at storage-type level using the minimum and maximum quantities maintained in the warehouse product master through transaction /SCWM/MAT1.

When the field is set to 1, replenishment is calculated separately for each fixed bin. In that case, the product-specific minimum and maximum quantities are maintained for each fixed-bin assignment through transaction /SCWM/BINMAT.

In this scenario, the Repl. Level field for storage type LRRH is blank. Therefore, SAP EWM considers the relevant stock across the storage type when calculating planned replenishment. A storage type can use either storage-type-level or fixed-bin-level replenishment; the two approaches cannot be applied simultaneously within the same storage type.

Master data:

#1 Storage type level Product Min/Max(/SCWM/MAT1)

Because storage type LRRH is configured for storage-type-level replenishment, the replenishment quantities are maintained in the warehouse product master using transaction /SCWM/MAT1.

For the selected product, the minimum quantity is maintained as 2 EA and the maximum quantity as 12 EA. During planned replenishment, SAP EWM checks the relevant stock available across storage type LRRH. When the stock falls below 2 EA, the system calculates the replenishment requirement by comparing the available quantity with the maximum quantity of 12 EA.

The minimum replenishment quantity is maintained as 4 EA. SAP EWM rounds the calculated replenishment quantity down to a multiple of 4 EA. Therefore, the final quantity may not always refill the storage type exactly to the maximum quantity.

The Planned Minimum Quantity and Planned Minimum Replenishment Quantity fields contain values proposed through slotting. In this example, both values are zero because no separate slotting proposal is being used. The manually maintained Minimum Quantity, Maximum Quantity, and Minimum Replenishment Quantity control the replenishment calculation.

#2 Available Stock : Product # XXX-75200-000(/SCWM/MON)

#3 Available Stock in Onsite Storage type –LRRH(/SCWM/MON)

There is no stock available for below bins associated with source storage type LRRH. Each bin capacity is fixed, so only 4 quantities can be stored for said product/material. Due to capacity constraint, each bin is accommodating 4 quantities and it is splitting the quantity from source bin.

Replenishment Execution(/SCWM/REPL):

During the planned replenishment run, SAP EWM calculates a replenishment requirement of 12 EA for product XXXXXX 75200-000 in destination storage type LRRH. Warehouse process type 3010 – Replenishment is determined based on the configured replenishment document and item types.

The WT Immed. indicator is selected. Therefore, SAP EWM immediately creates warehouse tasks when replenishment is executed. If this indicator were not selected, the system would first create or update the replenishment warehouse request, and warehouse tasks would have to be created in a separate step.

Although the requirement is calculated at storage-type level, SAP EWM must create executable warehouse tasks at storage-bin level. The system therefore determines the eligible source stock in LRRS and suitable destination bins in LRRH. The quantity is split when one source bin does not contain the complete requirement or one destination bin cannot accommodate the full quantity.

In this example, four warehouse tasks are created. Destination bin LRRH-BIN#7 receives quantities of 3 EA and 1 EA, LRRH-BIN#8 receives 4 EA, and LRRH-BIN#9 receives 2 EA. This split reflects the available stock in the selected source bins and the capacity available in each destination bin.

All four warehouse tasks are grouped into warehouse order 2001073645. Warehouse-order creation follows the applicable warehouse-order creation rule and considers criteria such as activity area, queue, route, consolidation group, weight, volume, number of tasks, and other configured limits. Because these warehouse tasks meet the same grouping criteria and do not exceed the WO limits, SAP EWM assigns them to one warehouse order for execution.

The calculated replenishment requirement is 12 EA, while the displayed warehouse tasks total 10 EA. This indicates that the requirement could only be fulfilled partially at the time of execution, most likely because of limited eligible source stock or available destination-bin capacity. The replenishment log and warehouse monitor should be checked to confirm the exact reason.

b) Fixed Bin Level: allows for precise replenishment control for each storage bin.

Best case use:

  • Fixed Bin Storage– Best for storage strategies where each product has dedicated bins
  • High-Value Items– Ensures exact replenishment when stock in a specific bin falls below the minimum threshold.
  • Different Bin Requirements - Useful when individual fixed bins require different minimum and maximum quantities within the planned replenishment process.

Limitations:

  •  Higher Maintenance– Requires setting up Min/Max for each bin, which can be time-consuming.
  •  Complexity in Large Warehouses. Managing thresholds for thousands of bins may become cumbersome.

Specific Configuration: Storage type LRRH

The Repl. Level field determines the level at which SAP EWM calculates the replenishment requirement. When this field is blank, replenishment is calculated at storage-type level using the minimum and maximum quantities maintained in the warehouse product master through transaction /SCWM/MAT1.

When the field is set to 1, replenishment is calculated separately for each fixed bin. In that case, the product-specific minimum and maximum quantities are maintained for each fixed-bin assignment through transaction /SCWM/BINMAT.

In this scenario, the Repl. Level field for storage type LRRH is blank. Therefore, SAP EWM considers the relevant stock across the storage type when calculating planned replenishment. A storage type can use either storage-type-level or fixed-bin-level replenishment; the two approaches cannot be applied simultaneously within the same storage type.

Master data:

#1 Fixed Bin with Product Min/Max(/SCWM/BINMAT)

For fixed-bin-level replenishment, the product is assigned to its destination bins and separate minimum and maximum quantities are maintained for each assignment using transaction /SCWM/BINMAT.

In this example, product XXX99902101 is assigned to two fixed bins in storage type LRRH. Bin LRRH-BIN#3 has a minimum quantity of 2 EA and a maximum quantity of 5 EA. Bin LRRH-BIN#2 has a minimum quantity of 1 EA and a maximum quantity of 3 EA.

During planned replenishment, SAP EWM checks the stock in each fixed bin separately. If the stock in BIN#3 falls below 2 EA, the system calculates replenishment toward 5 EA. If the stock in BIN#2 falls below 1 EA, it calculates replenishment toward 3 EA.

This approach allows each picking bin to have quantities based on its individual capacity and operational demand. It provides more precise control than storage-type-level replenishment, but it requires the product-bin assignments and quantities to be maintained separately for every fixed bin.

#2 Available Stock : Product # XXX A0199902101(/SCWM/MON)

#3 Available Stock in Onsite storage type -LRRH

Replenishment Execution(/SCWM/REPL):

Here replenishment will happen on the basis of min/max setting done at fixed bin level.

Although source bin quantity is splitting but destination bin quantity based on fixed bin min/max quantity.

During the planned replenishment run, SAP EWM evaluates each fixed bin independently. In this example, the system determines a replenishment requirement of 3 EA for destination bin LRRH-BIN#2 and 5 EA for destination bin LRRH-BIN#3.

Because the WT Immed. indicator is selected, SAP EWM creates the warehouse tasks immediately using warehouse process type 3010. The total replenishment requirement of 8 EA is divided into five warehouse tasks based on the available stock quants in the reserve storage type.

For LRRH-BIN#2, three warehouse tasks of 1 EA each are created. For LRRH-BIN#3, the requirement of 5 EA is fulfilled through two warehouse tasks: 2 EA from LRRS-BIN#1 and 3 EA from LRRS-BIN#4.

Although five warehouse tasks are created, they are grouped into a single warehouse order, 2001073651. This grouping is controlled by the applicable Warehouse Order Creation Rule and its limits and filters.

Important consideration:

#1 Storage type – Replenishment relevant

The Repl. Level field determines the level at which SAP EWM calculates the replenishment requirement. When this field is blank, replenishment is calculated at storage-type level using the minimum and maximum quantities maintained in the warehouse product master through transaction /SCWM/MAT1.

When the field is set to 1, replenishment is calculated separately for each fixed bin. In that case, the product-specific minimum and maximum quantities are maintained for each fixed-bin assignment through transaction /SCWM/BINMAT.

In this scenario, the Repl. Level field for storage type LRRH is blank. Therefore, SAP EWM considers the relevant stock across the storage type when calculating planned replenishment. A storage type can use either storage-type-level or fixed-bin-level replenishment; the two approaches cannot be applied simultaneously within the same storage type.

  • If Repl Level is “1” then replenishment should be Storage type level.

  • If Repl Level is “ ” then replenishment should be Fixed bin type level.

If replenishment is executed, then depending upon above configuration, it will execute either Storage type or Fixed bin approach.

#2 There is one of the technical restriction wherein one storage type’s replenishment will have either storage type or Fixed bin.

#3 Storage type – Split During put-away + Early Cap. Check

Above two settings, during put-away system will check the bin capacity in advance and accordingly split and accommodate the quantity in respective bin.

Conclusion:

Planned replenishment in SAP EWM provides a structured way to move stock from reserve storage to picking areas based on defined minimum and maximum quantities. The process is executed and allowing warehouse users to review and initiate replenishment according to current stock requirements.

Maintaining the control quantities at storage-type level is suitable when simpler master-data maintenance and aggregated stock control are sufficient. Maintaining them at fixed-bin level is more appropriate when products have dedicated picking bins and precise bin-level replenishment is required.

Selecting the appropriate level helps balance maintenance effort with operational accuracy. With the configuration and master data described in this article, organizations can use planned replenishment to improve stock availability in picking areas and support consistent warehouse execution.

 Author: Naveen Chandra Sharma

entry.title: Manyat Thinking: Not Every Problem Needs a Notification — Designing Business Attention in SAP
entry.content:
Manyat Thinking: Not Every Problem Needs a Notification — Designing Business Attention in SAP S/4HANA

Business First. SAP Second.

Introduction

In SAP, we can detect many things.

  • A Goods Receipt can create an event.
  • A warehouse process can generate an exception.
  • Transportation tracking can identify a delay.
  • A customer requirement can become at risk.
  • A process can detect an unexpected change.

But one question should come before designing another notification:

Does this problem actually require human attention?

Because detecting a problem and notifying a person are two different decisions.

I started thinking about this from a simple Goods Receipt scenario, but the same logic can be applied across EWM, TM/GTT, SD, MM, Procurement and other business processes.

1. It Started With a Simple GR Scenario

Imagine a Purchase Order for 100 units. The warehouse receives only 60 units.

The first reaction could be:

But should Procurement immediately receive a notification? Not necessarily.

Suppose the supplier has already confirmed: "The remaining 40 units will arrive tomorrow." And the customer also needs the material tomorrow. There is a quantity difference, but there may be no immediate business exception:

The transaction did not change. The business context changed. That is where notification design becomes interesting.

2. Event Is Not an Exception

A system event simply tells us: something happened. But the business needs to know: does this matter?

Therefore:

Event ≠ Business Exception

But even when a business exception exists, another question remains: does someone actually need to act? This gives us a broader decision logic:

 

Exception ≠ Notification

3. The First Filter: Can the Existing Process Handle It?

This became one of the strongest checks during my analysis.

Suppose TM detects a transportation problem. Before creating another notification, I would first ask:

Is the existing TM/GTT visibility and transportation process already providing the required handling?

For example, GTT/TM may already provide transportation visibility such as vehicle tracking, location, ETA, transportation events, and shipment visibility.

If the responsible transportation process can already manage the situation through its existing capabilities, then creating another notification simply because a problem was detected may add no value.

If the responsible process already provides the required visibility and handling, don't create another notification just because an exception exists.

Manyat Principle:

Let the responsible process handle what it is already designed to handle.

4. GTT: Visibility Is Not Automatically Notification

Transportation makes this distinction very clear.

Suppose Customer Commitment = 6:00 PM, Current ETA = 5:30 PM. GTT is already tracking the truck, and TM already has the transportation visibility.

Why should someone receive "Truck ETA is 5:30 PM" when that information is already available? Think about the difference:

Visibility ≠ Notification

Even if traffic data predicts that the ETA could move beyond the customer deadline, that is initially a risk signal — it does not automatically mean a business exception has occurred.

If later the carrier confirms a breakdown and the ETA becomes 7:15 PM, the business situation has materially changed. The question should therefore not simply be "Did GTT detect something?" The better question is "Does someone now need to take action?"

5. What About Changing the Truck?

Suppose Truck A becomes unavailable and TM assigns Truck B:

Should SD receive a notification? No. Changing the truck is part of TM's transportation responsibility — TM handles it. EWM may receive the updated transportation information through the normal process or integration if it needs that information for execution.

But turning every normal transportation change into a notification creates unnecessary noise.

Principle:

Normal process handling should remain normal process handling. A change by itself does not automatically justify a notification.

6. Detection Does Not Decide the Recipient

Now consider a warehouse availability issue. EWM identifies: Alternate Warehouse Stock = 5 EA, Reserved Stock = 3 EA, Actually Free = 2 EA.

EWM has detected the availability conflict. But the real business question may be: how will we fulfil the customer's commitment? That decision may belong to SD. SD may coordinate with MM/Procurement for additional supply, and EWM may execute the resulting warehouse activity later.

Detection ≠ Ownership

The process that detects the exception is not necessarily the process that should receive the notification.

7. Notification Recipient and Resolution Team Can Be Different

The person receiving the notification does not necessarily have to be the only person involved in solving the problem.

SD may coordinate with MM/Procurement for supply, TM for transportation, and EWM for warehouse execution.

The notification recipient and the people involved in resolution do not have to be the same.

The notification should reach the person who needs to make or initiate the next meaningful business decision or action.

8. EWM Exception Handling: Not Every Exception Needs Another Alert

EWM already provides exception-handling capabilities for warehouse execution. Warehouse tasks can encounter operational deviations, and EWM can react to those exceptions according to the configured process.

Suppose there is no customer impact, no escalation, no business decision, no manual intervention — then why create another notification? The exception may still be useful as operational, audit or analytical information where appropriate.

Important distinction:

Exception data does not automatically mean exception notification.

9. POSC Shows Another Side of the Same Thinking

The same principle can be seen with Process-Oriented Storage Control (POSC):

If the business requires mandatory process steps or control points, POSC can help control the expected warehouse process. But should every POSC step generate a notification? No — because POSC and notification solve different problems.

Process control manages execution. Notification manages attention.

If POSC is already controlling the required warehouse sequence, creating notifications for every normal process step would simply turn process execution into noise.

10. What If the Problem Solves Itself?

Consider: EWM detects an allocation issue, the system automatically corrects it, no customer impact, no manual intervention, no business decision.

Should somebody receive a notification? Not necessarily. The event or exception may still be retained for analysis, audit or trend monitoring where appropriate, but disturbing a person is unnecessary if there is no action to take.

Manyat Principle:

A self-resolved exception may need a record, but it does not necessarily need a notification.

11. Risk Is Not Automatically an Exception

Consider: Customer Requirement = 6:00 PM, Current ETA = 5:30 PM, Predicted ETA = 6:20 PM.

Should we immediately notify someone? Not necessarily — this is a risk signal, and the commitment has not necessarily been breached. Later:

Now the situation is materially different.

Risk Signal ≠ Business Exception

A monitoring system can continuously observe risk without continuously interrupting people.

12. Physical Reality Matters

Consider: Customer Order = 100, Goods Received = 100, Picking Complete, Packing Complete, Goods Physically Ready in Staging. Then the customer cancels the order.

The document changes. But does the physical warehouse movement disappear? No — the goods are still physically in the warehouse.

Document Cancellation ≠ Physical Movement Reversal

This is important in warehouse architecture because business documents and physical execution do not always change at exactly the same moment. Before designing a notification, understand the physical reality as well as the system state.

13. Existing Capability Before New Design

This became one of my strongest checks against overengineering.

Suppose an unplanned warehouse or yard requirement appears. Before creating a new notification mechanism, ask:

Does SAP already provide a capability for this scenario?

For example, an unplanned yard or warehouse movement may be handled through existing Ad-Hoc capabilities, depending on the specific process and configuration.

Manyat Principle:

Before designing something new, check what already exists.

14. The Notification Decision Framework

After going through these scenarios, I would use the following sequence:

The last option is important. Sometimes the correct design is nothing.

15. Where Does Situation Handling Fit?

SAP Situation Handling provides useful building blocks for this type of design. Depending on the specific SAP product, release and situation type, it can work with concepts such as conditions, situation instances, recipient determination, teams and responsibilities, notification settings, monitoring, and notification aggregation.

This means the technical capability can support a separation between business conditions and the eventual notification strategy. Instead of:

the thinking can become:

The exact capabilities and available fields depend on the specific SAP product, release and situation type, so the technical implementation still needs validation.

16. Notification Aggregation

There is another useful capability when notification volume genuinely becomes a problem.

Suppose Procurement has 3 Quantity Exceptions, 2 Supplier Confirmation Issues, and 5 Other Relevant Situations. Sending ten separate notifications may create unnecessary noise.

But aggregation should be an optimization, not the first answer to every notification problem:

 

Grouping should reduce noise, not reduce responsiveness.

17. The Architecture I Would Start With

Rather than beginning with "Which notification do we configure?" I would start with:

Only after this should we ask about the SAP technical implementation.

18. The Real Goal

The goal of a notification system should not be Maximum Notifications. It should be Maximum Relevance.

 

These situations are different. But they all lead to the same question:

Does somebody actually need to do something?

19. My Final Manyat Principle

After looking at these scenarios, I would summarize the thinking like this:

 

A problem is not automatically a notification.

First understand the problem. Then understand the business impact. Then check whether the responsible process can already handle it. Then identify who owns the next meaningful action. Only then decide whether human attention is required. And only after that should we design the notification mechanism.

Conclusion

The objective should not be to make SAP notify people about everything. The objective should be to make SAP provide the right information, to the right process, at the right time, with the right level of human attention.

Sometimes that solution will be Notification. Sometimes Monitoring. Sometimes Tracking. Sometimes Standard exception handling. Sometimes Aggregation. And sometimes — Nothing.

Because doing nothing can also be a valid design decision when the existing process already handles the situation and no human intervention is required.

Don't start by designing the notification. Start by designing the business response.

If another business problem appears, don't simply add another notification. Understand the problem. Check the existing capability. Identify the owner. Decide whether human attention is actually required. Then design the simplest solution that solves the business need.

Manyat Thinking

Business First. SAP Second.

"The best automation is not the one that tells humans about everything. It is the one that knows when humans actually need to know."

Rahul Kumar | Manyat Thinking

entry.title: Smarter Slotting in SAP EWM: What If Products That Travel Together Could Live Together?
entry.content:
Smarter Slotting in SAP EWM: What If Products That Travel Together Could Live Together?

An idea for extending ML-based slotting with product affinity

Introduction

Warehouse slotting has always been about putting the right product in the right place. But as warehouses become more intelligent, perhaps the question should no longer stop there.

What if two products are both stored in the right area, but they are frequently picked together and located far apart?

From an individual product perspective, the slotting decision may be completely correct. From an order-picking perspective, however, there may still be room for improvement.

In my work around SAP EWM, I have often seen how a warehouse decision can look perfectly logical when we look at one product at a time. But warehouse operations rarely executed one product at a time. Pickers move through orders, and orders create relationships between products.

That made me think about whether we are sometimes optimizing the location of individual products without fully optimizing the journey created by the order.

This led me to an idea: could product affinity become another signal that complements SAP EWM’s existing Machine Learning–based slotting?

Not as a replacement for the existing slotting logic, but as another layer of intelligence on top of it.

I call this idea Smarter Neighbors.

SAP EWM can already use machine learning to answer an important warehouse question:

Where should this product live?

But there is another question warehouses deal with every day:

What products usually go together?

What SAP EWM Already Does

SAP EWM’s Slotting by Machine Learning is already a useful capability. Through SAP’s Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) framework, it can analyze warehouse and product data and propose storage parameters such as the Storage Type Indicator, Storage Section Indicator, and Putaway Control Indicator.

The idea is straightforward: instead of manually deciding how a product should be classified based on expected movement and characteristics, the model learns from existing warehouse data and recommends an appropriate storage concept.

That is a meaningful step forward.

But the question I started exploring is whether the product itself is only one part of the story.

Because a warehouse does not ultimately pick products in isolation.

It picks orders.

What If We Looked at the Relationship Between Products?

Consider two products, Product A and Product B.

Both are fast movers, so the ML model can correctly identify them and place them in the appropriate fast-pick area.

Now imagine that 70% of the orders containing Product A also contain Product B.

If A is located at one end of the fast-pick area and B is at the other, the picker still must walk between them.

Both products were individually slotted correctly.

But the relationship between them was not considered.

This is where product affinity becomes interesting.

Instead of asking only:

“How fast does this product move?”

We could also ask:

“Which other products does this product usually move with?”

Product affinity, or correlated slotting, uses historical order patterns to identify products that frequently occur together. Those relationships could then potentially be used to position products closer to each other.

The objective isn’t simply to find products that are popular. It is to understand which products repeatedly participate in the same warehouse journeys.

A Different Layer of Intelligence: “Smarter Neighbors”

I think of this idea as Smarter Neighbors.

The existing ML-based slotting model could continue deciding the type of location a product should have — for example, fast-pick, bulk, or slower-moving storage.

An additional affinity layer could then look at order history and help optimize the physical proximity of products within that broader zone.

In simple terms:

ML slotting could decide the neighborhood, while affinity could help decide the neighbors.

That distinction is important to me.

I would not want affinity to override the fundamental storage strategy. A product should not suddenly move to a completely different storage area simply because it is frequently ordered with another product.

Instead, affinity could act as an additional signal for optimizing placement within an appropriate storage concept.

This creates a two-level decision:

Storage strategy → Where should the product live?

Product affinity → Who should it live closer to?

How Could It Work?

The first step would be to analyze confirmed outbound order history and identify which products frequently appear on the same orders.

From this data, we could calculate an affinity score between products and identify strong relationships.

For example, if Product A and Product B repeatedly appear together across a significant number of orders, the system could recognize that relationship and consider it when determining their final placement.

The existing slotting logic would still determine the broader storage concept.

Affinity would then become another input when deciding where the product should ideally sit within that zone.

There is also an important rule for situations where the two signals disagree.

Suppose Product A is a very fast mover, while its strongest affinity partner, Product B, is a slow-moving product.

It probably would not make sense to move Product B into the fast-pick area simply because the two products are frequently ordered together.

So, my initial thinking would be simple:

Velocity and product characteristics determine the storage zone; product affinity helps optimize proximity within that zone.

This separation could also make the approach easier to govern. The warehouse can retain the existing storage logic while using affinity as a controlled optimization layer.

Why I Think of the Separation Matters

From a practical EWM perspective, I would be cautious about making this an automated relocation mechanism from day one.

A mathematically strong affinity relationship does not automatically mean that two products should be physically adjacent.

There may be other considerations:

  • Storage capacity
  • Replenishment frequency
  • Product dimensions and weight
  • Handling requirements
  • Hazardous-material restrictions
  • Equipment requirements
  • Temperature or storage conditions
  • Operational constraints
  • Warehouse supervisor experience

A model may identify a strong relationship between two products, but the warehouse still needs to decide whether that relationship is operationally meaningful.

That is why I see Smarter Neighbors as a recommendation layer first, rather than an autonomous relocation mechanism.

The system could identify the relationship, propose a placement adjustment, and allow warehouse operations to validate the recommendation before execution.

The Interesting Part: SAP Already Has Some of the Building Blocks

This is also why I think the idea is worth exploring from an SAP perspective.

SAP’s existing ML capabilities around EWM use the ISLM framework, while HANA’s Predictive Analysis Library (PAL) provides analytical capabilities that include association-rule mining such as Apriori-based algorithms.

Association-rule mining is designed to identify relationships and co-occurrence patterns in datasets.

And that is essentially what we are trying to understand here:

Which products tend to appear together?

So, this isn’t necessarily about inventing completely new technology.

It could be about applying existing analytical capability to another warehouse problem.

The interesting question is how such a capability could relate to the existing EWM slotting process in a way that remains practical, explainable, and operationally controlled.

Could This Become Another ML Signal for Slotting?

This is where I see an interesting product opportunity.

Today, intelligent slotting can largely be thought of at a product level:

  • How fast does the item move?
  • What are its physical characteristics?
  • What storage concept does it require?
  • What storage parameters should be assigned?

What if future intelligent slotting could consider another dimension:

How do products behave together in actual customer orders?

The recommendation could potentially move beyond simply saying:

Put Product A in Zone X.

It could say something more like:

Put Product A in Zone X, preferably closer to Products B and C because they frequently travel together.

That would introduce a different dimension of intelligence into slotting.

The system would not only understand the characteristics and movement of an individual product.

It would begin to understand the relationship between products within the order flow.

Where Would I Start with a Pilot?

I wouldn’t try this across an entire warehouse initially.

I’d start with an area where multi-line orders are common.

Potential candidates could include:

  • E-commerce
  • Kitting operations
  • Recurring B2B replenishment
  • Spare parts
  • Promotional product combinations

The pilot could compare the existing placement with an affinity-adjusted placement while keeping the underlying product classification unchanged.

The primary measurement could be simple:

Pick-path distance per order.

Other useful measurements could include picker travel time, lines picked per hour, order cycle time, and potentially congestion within the picking area.

But I will start with one simple question:

Did the affinity-adjusted placement reduce the distance the picker had to travel?

If product classification remains unchanged but average travel distance decreases, that would provide an early indication that the additional affinity layer is contributing real value.

I would also want the pilot to run under controlled conditions. Product relocation should not happen simply because an algorithm identifies a correlation. The recommendation should be reviewed against warehouse constraints and operational experience.

Why Affinity Could Need a Different Learning Cycle

There is another aspect of this idea that I find particularly interesting.

Product velocity may change gradually, while product relationships can change much faster.

A promotion can suddenly cause two products to appear together frequently.

A new bundle can create a new relationship.

Seasonality can change order patterns.

Customer behavior can shift.

A product that historically had little relationship with another product may suddenly become a frequent companion.

This suggests that affinity could potentially have its own shorter retraining or recalculation cycle, without constantly changing the underlying storage strategy.

The warehouse could therefore maintain a relatively stable storage classification while allowing proximity recommendations to respond more dynamically to changes in actual order behavior.

Is This Already Being Done?

The concept of affinity-based or correlated slotting isn’t new in warehousing.

Similar principles are already used in areas such as market-basket analysis, warehouse optimization, and order-picking research.

What I am particularly curious about is the SAP EWM context.

Has anyone experimented with using order co-occurrence or association-rule analysis alongside standard EWM slotting?

For example, could this be explored through:

  • A custom BAdI
  • A side-by-side model on SAP BTP
  • HANA PAL
  • Custom analytics
  • A recommendation service
  • Or even a simpler analysis feeding recommendations back into the product or warehouse master data?

I would be very interested to hear how others have approached this.

Perhaps someone has already implemented a similar concept in an EWM environment, even if it wasn’t explicitly called “affinity-based slotting.”

Conclusion: From Smarter Products to Smarter Relationships

For me, the interesting part of this idea is not whether we can build another machine-learning model.

The technology to identify relationships between products already exists.

The more interesting question is whether we can use that intelligence in a way that complements the warehouse processes and controls already built into SAP EWM.

A product can be correctly classified based on its movement, physical characteristics, and storage requirements — and still be part of an inefficient picking journey because the products it frequently travels with are located far away.

That is where I see the potential of Smarter Neighbors.

The existing ML-based slotting logic could continue answering:

Where does this product belong?

An affinity layer could add another question:

Who should this product live next to?

Maybe the next step in intelligent slotting isn’t only teaching SAP EWM where a product belongs.

Maybe it’s also teaching the system which products belong together.

entry.title: Les vues du Material Master dans SAP : comment un seul objet sert tous les départements
entry.content:
1. Pourquoi des vues et pas une seule fiche ?

Un matériel n'a pas la même signification pour tous les services :

  • Pour les achats, c'est un article à commander, avec un fournisseur et un prix.
  • Pour la production, c'est un composant ou un produit fini avec une nomenclature et une gamme.
  • Pour les ventes, c'est un produit vendable avec un prix client et des conditions de livraison.
  • Pour la comptabilité, c'est une valeur de stock à valoriser au bilan.
  • Pour la qualité, c'est un objet soumis à un contrôle.

SAP a donc découpé le Material Master en vues indépendantes mais reliées entre elles, chacune alimentée par le service concerné, mais toutes rattachées au même numéro de matériel unique.

2. Les principales vues du Material Master

Vue Département responsable Contenu principal
Données de base (Basic Data)Data management / Gestion des données de baseDésignation, unité de mesure, poids, dimensions
Achats (Purchasing)AchatsGroupe d'acheteurs, texte de commande, délai
MRP (Planification des besoins)Planification / Supply ChainType d'approvisionnement, taille de lot, stock de sécurité
Production / Travail (Work Scheduling)ProductionCentre de production, temps de transit
Ventes (Sales)Ventes / Administration des ventesOrganisation commerciale, canal de distribution, statut de vente
Comptabilité (Accounting)Finance / ComptabilitéPrix standard, méthode de valorisation
Coûts (Costing)Contrôle de gestionClé de calcul des coûts, prix de revient
Stockage (Warehouse Management)Logistique / EntrepôtType de stockage, unité de manutention
Qualité (Quality Management)QualitéPlan de contrôle, certificat qualité

Chaque vue est facultative : un matériel n'a pas besoin d'avoir toutes les vues actives. Par exemple, un matériel purement acheté et revendu n'aura pas forcément de vue Production.

3. Le partage des données : les niveaux organisationnels

C'est ici que réside la véritable force du Material Master : les vues ne sont pas seulement fonctionnelles, elles sont aussi rattachées à des niveaux organisationnels différents. Cela permet à plusieurs sites, usines ou organisations commerciales d'utiliser le même matériel avec des paramètres propres.

3.1 Niveau Client (Mandant)

Les données valables pour toute l'entreprise, indépendamment du site :

  • Désignation du matériel
  • Groupe de marchandises
  • Unité de mesure de base

3.2 Niveau Organisation commerciale (Sales Org / Distribution Channel)

Spécifique aux ventes :

  • Prix de vente
  • Statut de distribution
  • Conditions commerciales

3.3 Niveau Usine (Plant)

Spécifique à chaque site de production ou de stockage :

  • Paramètres MRP
  • Données de production
  • Magasin par défaut

3.4 Niveau Magasin de stockage (Storage Location)

Le niveau le plus détaillé :

  • Emplacement de stockage
  • Règles de prélèvement

Exemple concret : un même matériel peut avoir un prix de vente différent selon l'organisation commerciale, un délai d'approvisionnement différent selon l'usine, tout en gardant la même désignation générale au niveau du mandant.

4. Comment cela fonctionne techniquement

D'un point de vue système, le Material Master repose sur plusieurs tables interconnectées :

  • MARA : données générales (niveau client)
  • MARC : données au niveau usine
  • MVKE : données au niveau organisation commerciale
  • MBEW : données de valorisation comptable
  • MARD : stocks par magasin

Chaque transaction de création ou modification (MM01, MM02, MM03) permet de sélectionner les vues à afficher ou modifier, ainsi que les niveaux organisationnels concernés (usine, organisation commerciale, etc.).

5. Les bénéfices de cette architecture

Une source unique de vérité : évite la duplication des données entre départements.

Une gouvernance claire : chaque service est responsable de sa propre vue, réduisant les erreurs de saisie croisées.

Une flexibilité multi-sites : un même produit peut avoir des paramètres différents selon l'usine ou le pays, sans créer de nouveaux matériels.

Une intégration native entre modules : les vues MRP, Production et Achats communiquent directement, ce qui fluidifie les processus de planification et d'approvisionnement.

6. Bonnes pratiques pour la gestion des vues

  1. Définir un processus de création clair (workflow d'approbation par département).
  2. Utiliser des rôles utilisateurs restreints : chaque département ne doit modifier que sa vue.
  3. Standardiser les extensions de matériel (extension à une nouvelle usine) via des templates ou des outils comme MM01 avec référence, ou des solutions de Data Governance (SAP MDG).
  4. Auditer régulièrement la cohérence inter-vues, notamment entre MRP et Production, pour éviter les ruptures de données.

Conclusion

Le Material Master illustre parfaitement la philosophie de SAP en matière de données maîtres : un objet unique, des responsabilités partagées. Grâce à son architecture en vues et en niveaux organisationnels, il permet à des départements aussi différents que les achats, la production, les ventes ou la finance de travailler sur la même donnée, chacun avec sa propre perspective, sans jamais perdre la cohérence globale de l'information.

Cette approche est un modèle de référence pour toute stratégie de gouvernance des données de base dans un environnement ERP complexe.

entry.title: Kit-to-Stock in SAP EWM with SAP PP Integration Configuration and End-to-End Process
entry.content:
Abstract

Kit-to-Stock is an SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM) process in which multiple component products are picked and assembled into a finished kit. The completed kit is received into warehouse stock and remains available for future sales orders or other business requirements. This process allows organizations to prepare frequently requested kits in advance, improving product availability and warehouse efficiency.

Introduction

In the Kit-to-Stock process, kits are created based on anticipated demand rather than for a specific customer order. The warehouse picks the required components, transfers them to a Value-Added Services (VAS) work center, performs the kitting activity, consumes the components, posts the completed kit and places it into storage.

In a decentralized SAP EWM scenario, the process can be initiated through an SAP ERP or SAP ECC production order. When the production order is released, an outbound delivery is created for the kit components, and an inbound delivery is created for the finished kit. These delivery documents are distributed to SAP EWM for warehouse execution.

The main benefits of Kit-to-Stock include:

  • Faster customer-order fulfillment
  • Reduced picking and packing time during order processing
  • Better control and visibility of component consumption
  • Improved availability of finished-kit inventory
  • Standardized kitting activities at the VAS work center
  • Integration between production-order processing and warehouse execution

Kit-to-Stock Process Flow

The following process flow illustrates how an SAP ECC production order initiates component staging and finished-kit receipt activities in decentralized SAP EWM.

Configuration

The following configuration is based on a decentralized SAP EWM system integrated with an SAP ECC system.

#1 Define order type(ECC)

SPRO->Production->Shop Floor control ->Master data ->Order->Define order types

A dedicated production order type, KTS1 – KIT TO STOCK, is configured for the Kit-to-Stock process. The order category is maintained as 10 (Production Order), which allows the order to use standard SAP production-order functionality.

The PP01 settlement profile is assigned for production-order cost settlement, while the CO partner update is maintained as Semi-active. Residence times are also defined to control how long completed orders remain in the system before they become eligible for archiving.        

#2 Production Scheduling profile(ECC)

SPRO->Production->Shop Floor control ->Master data ->Define Production Scheduling profile

The production scheduling profile KTS1 – KIT TO STOCK is maintained for plant XXXX. In the Transport section, the Kit to Stock in EWM indicator is selected, and production order type KTS1 is assigned under Make-to-Stock Production.

This indicator controls the integration between the production order and SAP EWM. When the production order is released, the system creates:

  • An outbound delivery for supplying and consuming the kit components.
  • An inbound delivery for receiving the completed kit header.

Both deliveries are then distributed to EWM for component picking, kit creation, goods receipt, and final put-away.

#3 Define relevance for VAS(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Cross process Settings ->VAS->Define relevance for VAS

This configuration connects the Kit-to-Stock VAS order with the corresponding EWM delivery documents for warehouse 1XXX. VAS order type KTS is assigned to order category D – VAS for Creating Kits for Stock.

For component processing, the system uses outbound document type OKTS with item type OKSR. For receiving the completed kit header, it uses inbound document type IKTS with item type IKSR. Stock type F2 is assigned to both document flows, and VAS procedure 0VSK controls the value-added service activities required for kit creation.

These settings allow EWM to create and process:

  • An outbound delivery order for picking and consuming the kit components.
  • An inbound delivery for receiving and putting away the completed kit.

#4 Document types for VAS for Kit to Stock(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Cross process Settings ->VAS->Document types for VAS for Kit to Stock

In this configuration, VAS order type KTS is assigned to order category D – VAS for Creating Kits for Stock for the applicable warehouse.

The following document and item types control the delivery flow:

  • OKTS / OKSR: Outbound delivery document and item types used for picking and consuming the kit components.
  • IKTS / IKSR: Inbound delivery document and item types used for receiving and putting away the completed kit header.
  • F2: Stock type assigned to both the outbound and inbound processes.
  • 0VSK: VAS procedure that controls the activities required to create the kit.

This configuration enables EWM to connect the component outbound process with the finished-kit inbound process under the same Kit-to-Stock VAS order.

#5 Map Document types from ERP system to EWM(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Interfaces->ERP Integration->Delivery processing -> Map Document types from ERP system to EWM

This configuration maps the delivery types received from the connected ERP business system to the corresponding EWM document types.

For the Kit-to-Stock process:

  • ERP inbound delivery type HID is mapped to EWM inbound document type IKTS.
  • ERP outbound delivery type HOD is mapped to EWM outbound document type OKTS.
  • The entries containing KTS provide Kit-to-Stock-specific mapping for the same inbound and outbound document flows.

When the production order is released, these mappings ensure that the ERP inbound and outbound deliveries are created in EWM with the correct Kit-to-Stock document types.

#6 Map Item types from ERP system to EWM(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Interfaces->ERP Integration->Delivery processing -> Map Item types from ERP system to EWM

This configuration maps the ERP delivery item types to the corresponding EWM item types for the Kit-to-Stock process.

  • For the inbound process, ERP document type HID and item type HIDN are mapped to EWM document type IKTS and item type IKSR. This item represents the completed kit header that will be received and put away in EWM.
  • For the outbound process, ERP document type HOD and item type HODN are mapped to EWM document type OKTS and item type OKSR. This item represents the components that will be picked and consumed during kit creation.

The CW Product indicator remains unchecked because catch-weight processing is not required for these materials.

Together with the document-type mapping, this setup ensures that ERP delivery items are created in EWM with the correct Kit-to-Stock item types.

End to End transaction flow:

#1 Finish product material –Tcode MM03(ECC)

#2 Production order - Kit to stock (ECC)

Kit to order (KTS1) was created and released using tcode CO01/CO02

Component display(ECC)

Displayed using tcode CO03.

After releasing the production order, outbound delivery was created for component consumption and inbound delivery for finish product.

#3 Outbound delivery for components (ECC)

Outbound delivery was displayed using tcode VL06O.

#4 Inbound delivery for Finish product(ECC)

 Inbound delivery was displayed using tcode VL06I.

\

#5 Outbound delivery for components(EWM)

Execution:

Outbound delivery displayed using /SCWM/PRDI with reference to Production order # 1476100.

Picking of Component (EWM)

Outbound delivery was Picked using tcode /SCWM/PRDI.

Outbound delivery status after Picking (EWM)

Outbound delivery status after Picking and displayed using /SCWM/PRDO.

Outbound delivery status (EMW)

Outbound delivery was goods issues and displayed using tcode /SCWM/PRDO.

Outbound delivery status (ECC)

outbound delivery PGId and displayed with tcode VL03N.

#6 Inbound delivery for Finish product (EWM)

Inbound delivery was displayed using /SCWM/PRDI against Production order # 1476100.

Inbound delivery status (ECC)

Displayed using tcode VL33N.

Conclusion

Kit-to-Stock integrates SAP PP and SAP EWM to support the advance assembly of component materials into a finished kit. When the production order is released in ECC, the system creates an outbound delivery for the kit components and an inbound delivery for the finished kit. These documents are transferred to EWM, where the warehouse performs component picking, consumption posting, kit creation, goods receipt, and final put away.

The process provides clear visibility across the complete document flow, from the production order in ECC to warehouse execution in EWM. With the correct production scheduling profile, VAS settings, document-type mapping, item-type mapping, and warehouse-process configuration, organizations can prepare frequently required kits in advance and reduce processing time during customer-order fulfilment.

 Author: Naveen Chandra Sharma
