SAP Joule in Supply Chain – Key Insights to be considering for support your start point with Joule

Overview

SAP Joule is rapidly transforming how supply chain professionals interact with enterprise systems. As SAP's generative AI copilot, Joule is embedded across key supply chain applications — from SAP Integrated Business Planning (IBP) and SAP S/4HANA Inventory Management to Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) and Procurement — enabling users to execute tasks, retrieve insights, and navigate applications using natural language.

With Joule now supporting over 50 domain-specific assistants backed by more than 200 specialized agents, and with Joule Studio reaching general availability in Q1 2026, supply chain teams are at a pivotal moment to adopt, configure, and govern Joule effectively.  This blog consolidates the most critical OSS Notes and architecture guidance every supply chain consultant and administrator should know.

Agentic AI & AI Agents | SAP Architecture Center

Product Sunset: Joule Embedded Entitlement (OSS Note 3720360)

What is happening?

SAP has announced the product sunset of the Joule Embedded Entitlement (SKU 8018168) in SAP Cloud Test, Demo, and Development (TDD) environments. Subscribers to this entitlement have received — or will receive — an official email notification from SAP confirming that the subscription will not be renewed at the end of the current subscription term.

Successor Offerings

SAP is directing customers and partners to transition to the following successor SKUs, which expand capabilities beyond the retiring entitlement:

SKU

Description

8020592

Cloud Test, Demo, and Development for Joule Base

8019670

Cloud Test, Demo, and Development for SAP AI Unit

Impact on Supply Chain Teams

Supply chain teams using TDD environments to prototype or validate Joule-enabled scenarios — such as inventory management automation, procurement workflows, or IBP planning assistants — must take action before their subscription term ends. Critically, existing embedded Joule configurations and entitlements will NOT automatically migrate to the successor offerings. Manual steps are required.

Recommended Actions

  • Review your current TDD subscription status on SAP for Me (me.sap.com)
  • Identify all active Joule Studio projects, custom skills, and SBPA (SAP Build Process Automation) tenant configurations that need to be exported or backed up before migration
  • Procure the successor entitlements (8020592 and/or 8019670) through your SAP account executive
  • Plan the manual reconfiguration of Joule Studio components in the new environment
  • Reference OSS Note 3720360 on SAP Support Portal for the full migration checklist

🔗 OSS Note: 3720360 – Product Sunset Announcement for Joule Embedded Entitlement (8018168)

Support Component Selection for Joule (OSS Note 3798165)

Why Component Selection Matters

Raising a support ticket under the wrong component is one of the most common causes of delayed resolution for Joule issues. OSS Note 3798165 provides definitive guidance on how to select the correct support component when experiencing Joule conversation or prompt-related issues.

Key Component Values

Based on the guidance aligned with this note and related Joule support documentation, the following component structure applies:

Scenario

Support Component

Joule capability issues in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (navigational/transactional)

CA-FLP-EXT-PCE-JOULE

Joule provisioning and entitlement issues

CA-JOULE-PRV

Custom skills built via Joule Studio / SAP Build

CA-BLD-JLE-SKI

Supply Chain Relevance

For supply chain teams, the most common prompt and conversation issues arise in:

  • Inventory Management (goods receipts, stock overview, material documents) component CA-FLP-EXT-PCE-JOULE
  • Procurement (purchase requisitions, purchase orders, supplier invoices) same component
  • SAP IBP (supply planning, lead time intelligence) verify the IBP-specific Joule component via SAP for Me

Important Distinction: Many Joule issues in supply chain stem from missing OData service activations or incorrect business role assignments, not from product defects. Before raising a ticket, verify OData activation status using SAP Note 3746234 (Role and OData Analyzer).

🔗 OSS Note: 3798165 – How to select the correct support component for Joule conversation/prompt issues

Joule Architecture & Security (OSS Note 3786517 + Reference Architecture)

Architecture Overview

OSS Note 3786517 provides the official Joule architecture and security guide. This is complemented by the SAP Architecture Center reference architecture for Identity and Access Management (IAM) for SAP Joule, available at:

🔗 https://architecture.learning.sap.com/docs/ref-arch/ea5d4f

At its core, the Joule architecture positions the AI copilot at the center of a layered integration model:

 

Identity and Access Management (IAM) Key Architectural Values

The IAM reference architecture for Joule establishes the following critical integration points:  

  1. SAP Cloud Identity Services – Identity Authentication (IAS): Joule relies on a configured trust relationship between the SAP BTP subaccount and the IAS tenant. This is a mandatory prerequisite for all Joule deployments.
  2. User Attribute Configuration: User attributes must be configured for Joule from the Identity Directory within IAS. This ensures that Joule inherits the correct user context and entitlements.
  3. Joule Booster: The Joule Booster on SAP BTP automates the setup of the Joule Formation, including the communication scenario SAP_COM_0882 for S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition integration.
  4. Role-Based Access Control: Joule inherits the user's existing SAP entitlements — users cannot query data they are not authorized to see. This is enforced at the backend application layer, not within Joule itself.

Joule Extensibility Architecture — Four Capability Patterns

The SAP reference architecture for Integrating and Extending Joule (Ref-Arch 464deb) defines four canonical capability patterns:

Pattern

Description

Supply Chain Example

Natural language triggers direct backend processes

Create goods receipt, post inbound delivery

Navigational

Guides users to the right Fiori app

"Where can I manage warehouse tasks?"

Informational

Delivers knowledge via RAG from indexed documents

Query delivery notes from SharePoint

Analytical

Surfaces business insights on demand

Lead time intelligence in IBP

Security Considerations for Supply Chain Deployments

  • All Joule integrations must route through SAP Cloud Identity Services — direct backend connections without IAS trust are not supported
  • For SAP IBP integrations, verify the integration path via the Joule Onboarding Guide to ensure the Joule Formation status displays "Ready"
  • For SAP Ariba integrations, an additional entitlement and authorization may be required — consult your account executive
  • BTP subaccount setup must include correct Global Account, subaccount, and entitlement configuration before running the Joule Booster

🔗 OSS Note: 3786517 – Joule Architecture and Security Guide 🔗 IAM Reference Architecture: https://architecture.learning.sap.com/docs/ref-arch/ea5d4f

Joule Studio Setup with SAP Build Apps (OSS Note 3733441)

What is Joule Studio?

Joule Studio, available within SAP Build, is a low-code/no-code environment for creating, deploying, monitoring, and managing custom Joule skills and agents. It reached general availability in Q1 2026 and is the primary tool for extending Joule with supply chain-specific capabilities.  

Prerequisites for Configuring Joule Studio (OSS Note 3733441)

OSS Note 3733441 covers the prerequisites and setting up scenarios for configuring Joule Studio with SAP Build Apps. Based on the aligned architecture and provisioning guidance, the following prerequisites apply:  

BTP Platform Prerequisites:

  • Active SAP BTP Global Account with appropriate entitlements

entry.content:
Control Exceptions Without Blocking Everything: Weight Variance Across SAP EWM, TM, and Situation Handling

A Design Perspective on Risk-Based Discrepancy Handling Across Warehouse, Transportation, and Yard Operations

1. Introduction: The Business Problem

In supply chain operations, a weight discrepancy is not simply a difference between two numbers. It can affect transportation planning, vehicle capacity, warehouse execution, operational safety, and delivery commitments.

The important business question is not whether every difference should stop the process, but whether the difference requires intervention before the next activity proceeds.

Consider a shipment with a planned weight of 10,000 KG. During warehouse execution, the actual weight is recorded as 10,120 KG. The difference is 120 KG.

Should the shipment automatically be blocked?

Not necessarily. The answer depends on the applicable business tolerance, transportation requirements, and operational risk.

A blanket block can delay shipments unnecessarily. Ignoring every discrepancy can allow a genuine transportation or warehouse issue to continue without review.

The objective is to control the risk without creating unnecessary operational disruption.

SAP Transportation Management (TM), SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM), and Situation Handling can support different responsibilities within this approach. The design must use their respective capabilities without treating one component as a replacement for another.

2. SAP TM: Quantity Tolerance and Transportation Control

SAP TM provides condition-based quantity tolerance functionality for evaluating relevant changes in weight.

The following configuration objects are identified in SAP TM documentation for this purpose:

  • Condition type: /SCMTMS/CC_QUAN_TOL
  • Data access definition: /SCMTMS/TORQTYCHGWEI

The data access definition provides the weight-change value in kilograms. A condition decision table can classify changes according to configured thresholds.

For example, a business might consider a change of more than 100 KG relevant while treating smaller changes as non-relevant. This is an illustrative business threshold, not a universal SAP default.

However, classifying a weight change as relevant does not automatically mean that a freight order is blocked.

The condition, its use in the applicable Change Controller configuration, and the resulting action must be considered together.

SAP TM also supports transportation document blocks through configured block reasons and block profiles. The applicable profile must be assigned to the relevant document types, and the configured process logic must determine when a block is set.

Implementation References

  • Condition type: /SCMTMS/CC_QUAN_TOL
  • Data access definition: /SCMTMS/TORQTYCHGWEI
  • Configuration activity: SAP NetWeaver Business Client (NWBC) → Application Administration → General Settings → Conditions → Create Condition
  • Related configuration: Change Controller strategy, block reason codes, block profile, and assignment of the profile to relevant document types.

These configuration objects and activities must be checked against the target SAP TM release and solution scope.

The key distinction is that the tolerance condition identifies a relevant change, while the applicable control logic determines the response.

3. SAP EWM: Warehouse Execution and Weight Verification

SAP EWM has a separate responsibility: managing warehouse execution and recording the actual information available during the warehouse process.

For example, when handling units are received, weight information can be entered manually or obtained from a connected weighing device where the relevant process supports it.

Warehouse execution information can then be used to identify differences between expected and actual goods information.

EWM's applicable checks and controls must be selected according to the warehouse process and the type of discrepancy.

Quantity overdelivery tolerances, delivery quantity adjustments, and warehouse execution differences should not automatically be described as a universal weight-variance blocking mechanism. They address their respective configured processes.

In this design, EWM remains responsible for warehouse-side checks. It does not need to duplicate TM's transportation tolerance logic merely because the same physical goods are involved.

The same physical discrepancy can affect two systems without requiring both systems to perform the same control.

4. Connecting EWM Execution Information to SAP TM

SAP documents integration scenarios in which actual warehouse information is transferred from EWM to TM.

In supported delivery-based and transit-warehousing processes, actual quantities can be transferred, and differences from planned quantities can result in discrepancies in TM.

SAP also documents the transfer of discrepancies identified during EWM execution in transit warehousing. The resulting discrepancy can be displayed in relevant transportation documents and handled by the transportation planner or customer service agent.

This provides an integration foundation for warehouse execution information and transportation discrepancy management.

However, a quantity discrepancy and a weighbridge weight change are not interchangeable concepts.

For the proposed weight-variance scenario, the implementation must use a supported way of transferring or making the relevant actual weight available to TM.

If the standard integration in the selected release does not provide the required weight field or trigger for the intended process, an appropriate supported enhancement or integration design may be necessary.

Proposed End-to-End Flow

  1. TM provides the planned transportation information.
  2. EWM records the actual warehouse information through the applicable receiving or execution process.
  3. The supported integration makes the relevant actual information available to TM.
  4. TM evaluates the weight change through its configured tolerance and control logic.
  5. The applicable transportation control is applied when the configured conditions and process logic require it.
  6. The exception is communicated to the responsible user through a supported notification mechanism, where configured.

This is a proposed design flow using relevant SAP capabilities. The exact behaviour depends on the target SAP release, integration, and configuration.

5. Situation Handling: Attention Is Not Enforcement

A system restriction and a user notification solve different problems.

A block controls whether a particular business activity can proceed. A notification helps the responsible person understand that an exception needs attention.

Situation Handling can support exception awareness through configured situation scenarios, conditions, recipients, and supported actions.

It should not be presented as the mechanism that independently creates a TM transportation block.

The responsibilities in this design are:

Component Primary Responsibility
SAP TMTransportation-side tolerance evaluation and control
SAP EWMWarehouse execution information and applicable warehouse checks
Situation HandlingException awareness and user response through supported scenarios

For example, when a significant weight discrepancy meets the configured situation conditions, the responsible transportation planner or warehouse supervisor may be notified, depending on the scenario and recipient determination.

The user can investigate the reason, coordinate with the relevant team, and follow the applicable resolution process.

A notification should not be assumed to exist simply because a TM block or discrepancy has been created. The supported Situation Handling scenario and configuration must provide the required behaviour.

6. Risk Classification: Evaluate Before Blocking

A weight difference should not automatically trigger the same response in every situation.

The business must define how discrepancies are classified and what action is appropriate for each risk level.

The following matrix illustrates one possible business approach. These categories are proposed design criteria, not standard SAP risk levels.

Business Decision Matrix

Risk Level Business Situation Appropriate Response
LowDifference is within the approved tolerance and no separate risk existsContinue processing and record the difference
MediumDifference requires verification but does not justify an immediate stopNotify the responsible user and perform targeted verification
HighDifference exceeds the defined tolerance and requires investigationApply the configured control and escalate for review
CriticalA confirmed safety, security, legal, or other mandatory stop condition existsEnforce the required stop through the responsible control mechanism

Actual thresholds, responsible roles, escalation rules, and control actions must be defined according to business requirements.

A percentage threshold alone may not be sufficient. An absolute weight difference may also be significant, depending on shipment size and operational conditions.

Where percentage-based and absolute-weight thresholds indicate different risk levels, the design should apply the highest applicable risk classification unless an explicitly approved business rule specifies otherwise.

A mandatory safety, security, or legal stop condition must not be downgraded simply because the numerical weight difference is small.

Decision Flow

Detect Weight Difference
↓
Evaluate Business Tolerance
↓
Classify Risk
↓
Select the Appropriate Control
↓
Notify the Responsible User, Where Required
↓
Investigate and Resolve

This decision flow separates the business decision from the technical mechanism used to implement it.

7. End-to-End Example: From Weighbridge to Resolution

Consider this illustrative scenario.

Business Information Value
Planned transportation weight10,000 KG
Actual weight recorded10,120 KG
Weight difference+120 KG
Illustrative business tolerance100 KG
Difference classificationRelevant

The business has configured a tolerance rule under which this difference is considered significant.

Step 1: Record the Actual Weight

EWM records the actual weight through the applicable warehouse process.

Step 2: Make the Information Available to TM

The relevant information is made available to TM through the supported integration.

Step 3: Evaluate the Difference

TM evaluates the change according to its configured tolerance condition and the applicable transportation-control logic.

Step 4: Apply the Required Control

If the configured response requires a block and the process conditions are met, the relevant transportation document is restricted.

Step 5: Notify the Responsible User

Situation Handling can separately notify the responsible user when the discrepancy meets the configured situation conditions.

Step 6: Investigate and Resolve

The responsible user investigates the difference. Possible explanations include a recording error, an incorrect planned weight, a change in the goods, or another operational cause.

The business determines the appropriate resolution. Depending on the outcome and configured controls, the discrepancy may be corrected or accepted, and the applicable block may be removed by an authorized user or through supported process logic.

The result is not that every weight difference blocks the supply chain. It is that a significant exception can receive the appropriate transportation control and human attention while other activities remain subject to their own rules.

8. Implementation and SAP Documentation References

The implementation should reuse the SAP capabilities relevant to each responsibility instead of introducing a separate blocking mechanism for every component.

8.1 Configure the TM Quantity Tolerance

Use /SCMTMS/CC_QUAN_TOL and /SCMTMS/TORQTYCHGWEI where supported by the target TM release and process.

Configure the decision table to distinguish relevant from non-relevant weight changes according to the business tolerance.

8.2 Configure the Transportation Response

Configure the relevant Change Controller strategy and determine the intended response when a change is classified as relevant.

If a transportation block is required, configure the applicable block reason, block profile, and document-type assignment.

The tolerance condition must not be described as a hard block by itself. Block behaviour depends on the complete applicable configuration and process logic.

8.3 Configure Discrepancy Handling

Use the relevant TM discrepancy configuration when the process requires discrepancies to be recorded and resolved.

The implementation must determine which document and which activity should be restricted, rather than assuming that every discrepancy blocks all subsequent processing.

8.4 Validate EWM-to-TM Integration

Identify how actual weight is captured in EWM and how the relevant information reaches TM in the selected solution.

The specific weight field, integration trigger, and resulting TM action must match the proposed scenario. Any additional integration or enhancement requirement should be documented only after the standard capabilities for the target release have been assessed.

8.5 Configure Situation Handling Separately

Select a supported Situation Handling scenario that fits the business exception, where one is available.

Define the applicable conditions, recipients, and notification or action behaviour.

Situation Handling supports awareness and resolution; it is not a substitute for TM block configuration.

8.6 SAP Documentation

The following references provide relevant configuration and capability information:

  • Defining Conditions for Quantity Tolerances — SAP TM Configuration Guide
  • Blocking Information of Freight Units and Capacity Documents — SAP Help Portal
  • Handling Discrepancies in Transit Warehousing Process — SAP Help Portal
  • Delivery-Based Integration with SAP EWM — SAP Help Portal
  • Resolution of Discrepancies — SAP Help Portal

These references establish relevant SAP capabilities and configuration concepts. The exact implementation must match the selected release and business process.

9. Implementation Considerations

The proposed design must align with the SAP release, integration scope, and configuration available in the target system.

The relevant weight fields, integration triggers, tolerance conditions, transportation controls, and Situation Handling scenarios must be assessed according to the applicable business process.

The design should distinguish documented SAP capabilities from the configuration required to connect them into the intended business flow.

This ensures that each component has a clear responsibility and that the resulting implementation supports the intended business outcome.

10. Design Principle: Control Exceptions Without Blocking Everything

A business exception should trigger a response proportionate to its operational risk.

A discrepancy should not automatically block the entire process. The appropriate control should depend on the business requirement, the significance of the difference, and the consequences of proceeding.

In this design:

  • SAP TM manages transportation-side tolerance evaluation and controls.
  • SAP EWM manages warehouse execution and its applicable checks.
  • Situation Handling supports exception awareness and resolution.

The objective is not to remove controls, but to apply the right control at the right point without creating unnecessary operational disruption.

A discrepancy should receive the control it requires—not an automatic restriction simply because a difference exists.

11. Conclusion

A weight discrepancy should not automatically result in the same response in every situation.

The correct response depends on the business tolerance, operational risk, and responsibility of the affected system.

SAP TM provides transportation-side tolerance evaluation and blocking capabilities. SAP EWM provides warehouse execution information and applicable warehouse controls. Situation Handling can help bring supported exceptions to the right people.

The value of the design lies in connecting these responsibilities without confusing their purposes.

A relevant discrepancy can receive the required control and attention without turning every small difference into an unnecessary process-wide block.

The principle is simple: detect the exception, apply the appropriate control, and bring the right person into the resolution process.

Pick-by-Voice in EWM: The Problem Wasn’t the Voice - It Was What We Made It Say

Introduction

Pick-by-Voice in SAP EWM is one of those technologies that looks very simple when you see it working for the first time. The operator wears a headset, SAP EWM guides the picking process, the operator responds using voice commands, and the system moves to the next step. From a technical perspective, once the device, voice solution, RF transaction and SAP configuration are connected, it can feel like the difficult part is already behind you.

My experience was different.

On my first Pick-by-Voice project, the solution was technically working as expected. The device was connected, the RF transaction was functioning, the prompts were being played and the operators were able to respond. But shortly after go-live, I learned that a solution being technically correct does not necessarily mean that it is comfortable or efficient for the person using it.

One of the experienced pickers told me something very simple: “The headset is talking too much.”

That sentence changed the way I looked at Pick-by-Voice. The problem was not that the system could not speak. The problem was that we had made it say too much.

The Day I Realized the Problem Wasn’t the Voice

My first reaction was to think about the speech rate. If the system was speaking too much, perhaps we could make it speak faster. So, I discussed it with the voice vendor and we tried increasing the speech rate.

It sounded like a logical solution. It wasn't.

As the speech became faster, the voice interaction became less forgiving and the overall experience was not necessarily better. That was when I decided to stop looking at the problem from the system's perspective and actually experience it from the operator's perspective.

I put on the headset and went through the picking process myself.

The system was reading the source bin, the handling unit, the product, the quantity and the unit of measure. Technically, all of that information was correct. But when you are standing in a warehouse and trying to pick efficiently, hearing a long handling unit number read out completely is a very different experience.

The HU number was already available on the label in front of the operator. We did not necessarily need the system to speak every digit of a long number. The voice dialogue was technically complete, but operationally it was too verbose.

That led us to a much simpler question: Does the operator really need to hear this?

Instead of trying to make the voice talk faster, we started looking at what the voice actually needed to say.

In that project, we shortened the information being spoken, including using only the relevant part of the HU identification, and removed information that was not necessary for the operator at that point in the process. We also looked at the order in which information was presented.

Interestingly, this is not just a project-specific idea. SAP's standard Pick-by-Voice logic itself has HU validation designed to avoid making the operator speak the complete HU number. EWM can determine the minimum number of digits from the end of the HU number required to identify it uniquely within the storage bin.

The lesson for me was straightforward: the best voice optimization is not always speaking faster. Sometimes it is simply saying less.

That experience also made me look more closely at what is happening inside SAP EWM when a voice dialogue is running.

Where the Voice Conversation Actually Happens

SAP Pick-by-Voice is built around the EWM RF framework and the RF picking transaction, together with the ITS template generator for mobile devices with speech input. SAP EWM uses SAPGUI dynpros whose fields contain speech-related properties, and the system generates HTML templates containing speech-specific tags that are interpreted by the browser on the voice device.

The important point is that SAP EWM remains responsible for the warehouse process and RF dialogue, while the voice platform and device layer provide the speech interaction and recognition required by the solution. The exact architecture can vary depending on the voice solution being used.

This distinction matters when troubleshooting a voice issue.

When an operator says, “The voice is too slow,” “The system is asking for too much information,” or “It doesn't understand me,” the answer may not be to change something in the voice engine.

Sometimes the real issue is the SAP dialogue we designed.

The SAP EWM Controls Behind the Dialogue

SAP EWM provides several speech-related properties that influence how a field participates in the Pick-by-Voice dialogue. Among the key properties are PromptText, HelpText, FilledText, Grammar and GrammarLnk.

PromptText defines the text used to prompt the operator for input. HelpText can be spoken when the input is not recognized, while FilledText can be used after speech input has been successfully detected. Grammar defines the grammar used to recognize speech input, while GrammarLnk allows the grammar to be loaded externally. SAP documentation also describes attributes such as TimeOut and NextField, which can influence the speech dialogue flow.

SAP's Pick-by-Voice documentation states that a screen can contain up to ten prompts, grammars and help texts.

These properties give you considerable control over the conversation, but I don't think they should be treated simply as technical fields to be populated.

They determine what the warehouse operator hears and what the system expects the operator to say.

That makes them part of the warehouse user experience.

Using the BAdI to Change What the Operator Hears

One of the useful enhancement points for this is the Modify Screen Field Voice Properties BAdI.

SAP provides this BAdI under the EWM Mobile Data Entry area, and it can be used to change the voice properties of the screen and its fields before the screen is presented to the user. SAP introduced this BAdI specifically as part of the Pick-by-Voice functionality.

This is important because the voice dialogue does not always have to be completely static.

The voice properties can be influenced based on the actual process and data being handled. This gives you the flexibility to make the dialogue more relevant instead of forcing every operator through exactly the same amount of spoken information.

Going back to my HU example, if EWM knows the complete HU number, that does not automatically mean the operator needs to hear the complete number.

The technical question is:

What value does the field contain?

The business question is:

What does the operator actually need to hear?

Those are two different questions.

And that distinction is where a lot of the practical optimization happens.

Grammar Matters as Much as the Prompt

There is another side to the conversation that is easy to overlook: what the system expects the operator to say.

A good voice dialogue is not only about creating clear prompts. The grammar also needs to be designed carefully. If the expected vocabulary is unnecessarily broad or the grammar is complicated, the voice interaction can become harder to recognize and troubleshoot.

For example, a quantity field normally does not need a large vocabulary. The expected response is generally a number, together with whatever confirmation or help options the process requires.

Keeping the expected grammar focused makes the interaction more predictable.

Bin verification is another good example.

SAP's standard Pick-by-Voice functionality does not necessarily require the operator to repeat a complete storage bin. The storage bin can be split into components such as storage type, aisle, stack and level, with the appropriate validation used for each part. SAP also documents a mechanism where only the difference between the previous and current storage bin needs to be spoken when the relevant information remains unchanged.

The same principle applies to HU validation. SAP documents a specific PbV validation logic that can determine how many digits from the end of an HU number are required to uniquely identify it in the storage bin. For example, instead of speaking a complete HU number, the operator may only need to speak the required trailing digits.

This is exactly the kind of detail that demonstrates why voice dialogue should be designed together with the warehouse process.

The goal is not to make the system say everything it knows.

The goal is to make the operator say and hear only what is necessary.

Commands Are Part of the Conversation Too

Pick-by-Voice is not only about reading fields and accepting values. Commands are also part of the interaction.

SAP's Pick-by-Voice transaction supports commands that allow the operator to control the dialogue. The operator can enter command mode using the integrated Command keyword, and the Okay command corresponds to the Enter pushbutton. SAP also documents the use of voice-related properties and command buttons as part of the RF dialogue.

These details may sound small, but they become important when designing a voice process that feels natural.

The operator should not have to remember an unnecessarily complicated set of commands just to move through a standard picking flow.

Commands should support the process rather than become another process the operator has to learn.

What I Would Do Differently Today

If I were starting another Pick-by-Voice implementation today, I would involve the warehouse operators much earlier in the design of the dialogue.

Not just during UAT. Not just after the configuration is finished.

I would actually put the headset on during design and walk through the real picking process.

I would ask simple questions. What information do you need to hear? What information is already visible on the label? Which numbers are difficult to understand when spoken? Which prompts feel repetitive? Which responses are natural for the operator and which ones feel like something designed by a system rather than a person?

I would also test the dialogue at realistic warehouse speed.

A prompt that sounds perfectly reasonable when someone is sitting in a meeting room can feel completely different when the operator is moving through a warehouse, handling a pallet or carton and trying to maintain a picking rhythm.

That is probably the biggest lesson I took from my first project. Pick-by-Voice should be designed with the operator's ears in mind, not only the developer's screen.

Conclusion

Getting Pick-by-Voice technically connected to SAP EWM is an important part of the implementation, but it is not the end of the work.

The real challenge starts when you ask whether the conversation makes sense to the person wearing the headset.

My first instinct was to make the voice speak faster. The better solution was to make the system speak less. That experience changed how I look at voice implementations in EWM.

A prompt can be technically correct and still be a poor warehouse prompt. A grammar can be valid and still be unnecessarily complicated. A piece of information can be available in EWM and still not need to be spoken.

For me, the most important principle is simple:

Don't ask how much information the system can say. Ask how much information the operator actually needs to hear.

Pick-by-Voice works best when the technology stays in the background, and the dialogue feels natural to the person doing the work.

That is where the real optimization begins.

entry.title: One Business Exception, Different SAP Responsibilities
entry.content:
One Business Exception, Different SAP Responsibilities

Separating Evidence, Attention and Execution with GOS and Situation Handling

Principle 6: Separate Business Requirement From Technical Mechanism

The Real Business Problem

A warehouse exception can look very simple on the ground. An operator may find a weight variance, a broken seal, a damaged pallet, or a product condition that requires visual evidence.

The natural reaction is often to start thinking about the SAP object, notification, document, repository, or integration that should be used.

But the better starting point is the business situation itself.

What does the business actually need at that moment?

Consider a simple broken-seal scenario. An operator receives a pallet and discovers that its seal is broken. The operator takes a photograph as evidence.

At this point, several different requirements exist.

The photograph is evidence. Someone needs to know that the exception requires attention. A physical action may follow, which is execution. Later, the business may need to understand what actually happened, which is history.

These requirements are connected, but they are not the same requirement.

That distinction is where the architecture should begin.

What Is the Business-First Design Approach?

The business-first design approach starts with the physical situation, asks WHY, identifies the actual business requirement, and only then maps that requirement to the appropriate SAP capability and technical implementation.

The thinking flow is:

Ground Reality → Exception → WHY → Root Cause → Business Requirement → Business Decision → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation → Practical Application

This is not intended to replace standard SAP solution architecture or introduce a new SAP methodology.

It is simply a practical way of approaching an SAP problem from the business side first.

The core question is:

What does the business actually need, and which SAP capability naturally owns that requirement?

A Worked Example: Broken Seal

The operator has found a broken seal.

The first requirement is evidence. The photograph needs to remain associated with the relevant business context. Where supported by the relevant business object/application, GOS or the applicable attachment capability can provide that function.

The second requirement is attention. The photograph itself does not determine who needs to act. Situation Handling has a different responsibility: bringing the relevant business situation to the attention of the responsible user.

The third requirement is action. Suppose the responsible user decides that the affected HU must be moved to a clarification or quarantine area. The physical warehouse movement belongs to the existing EWM execution process.

The fourth requirement is history. After the warehouse action is completed, the business may need to know what happened, when it happened, and what warehouse execution was confirmed.

So the architecture becomes:

Evidence → GOS / Attachment → Situation Handling → Warehouse Action → EWM Execution → EWM Warehouse Task History

This is the important architectural separation.

The problem is not really a single "notification/document" problem. It is several business requirements that happen to originate from the same physical exception.

Business Requirement → SAP Capability

Once the requirements are separated, the mapping becomes much clearer.

Business Requirement SAP Capability Technical Reference

Store visual evidenceGOS / AttachmentGOS capability where supported by the relevant business object/application
Bring exception to responsible userSituation HandlingManage Situation Types — F2947
Execute warehouse actionExisting EWM process / Warehouse TaskDepends on process design
Record confirmed warehouse executionEWM Warehouse Task History/SCWM/ORDIM_C
Structured enterprise document managementDMSWhen a genuine DMS requirement exists

This table is not intended to replace the architecture. It makes the responsibility of each capability visible.

The important relationship is:

Business Requirement → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation

That is the point where business thinking connects with SAP implementation.

One Business Situation, Different SAP Responsibilities

A common design mistake is to make one technical mechanism responsible for everything simply because all the information came from the same exception.

That is not necessary.

GOS / Attachment can maintain the supporting evidence where the relevant business object supports it. Situation Handling can bring the business situation to the responsible user. EWM can execute the physical warehouse movement through its existing process. EWM execution history can provide the record of confirmed warehouse execution.

The capabilities work together, but they do not need to become one combined technical layer.

This is also why a notification should not automatically become an evidence repository, and an evidence repository should not automatically become the warehouse execution mechanism.

Direct Access: The Speed Layer

A user receiving a situation should not have to search through unrelated repositories simply to understand the exception.

The practical path should be as direct as the scenario allows:

Situation → Relevant Business Context → Evidence → Decision

Situation Handling provides the attention. GOS provides the evidence where supported by the relevant business object/application. EWM provides the physical execution.

The exact navigation or action available to the user depends on the Situation Handling scenario, business object, application and configuration.

In this article, I use "speed layer" as a design term for the shortest practical path from a business situation to its supporting evidence. It is not an SAP product name or a standard SAP architectural layer.

The principle is simple:

Do not create another technical layer merely to make information reachable when the existing business context can already provide the required path.

When the Business Says: "We Need History"

One of the easiest ways to overengineer an architecture is to say:

"We need history."

The next question should immediately be:

"History of what?"

If the business needs the photograph, it needs evidence. If it needs to know what warehouse movement occurred, it needs execution history. If it needs to know who was responsible for the situation, it needs situation and responsibility information. If it genuinely needs an enterprise document-management lifecycle, DMS may become relevant.

The word history by itself is not enough to determine the technical solution.

This becomes especially important for audit requirements.

An audit question may be: What did the operator see? What evidence was captured? Who performed the action? When did it happen? What warehouse movement was executed? Why was the decision taken?

These questions describe different types of information.

Therefore: audit requirement does not automatically mean DMS.

The better question is:

"What story does the audit need to reconstruct?"

If that story is already represented across the business situation, business object, supporting evidence and execution history, another repository may simply duplicate information rather than solve a new requirement.

DMS becomes relevant when the business genuinely requires structured document-management capabilities beyond what the existing business objects and processes provide.

When the Pattern Changes

This approach does not mean that GOS should always be used, Situation Handling should always be used, or DMS should never be used.

The requirement determines the capability.

A transportation exception may require TM capabilities. A maintenance-related requirement may require EAM capabilities. A warehouse execution requirement may require EWM capabilities. A genuine enterprise document-management requirement may require DMS.

The technical objects change according to the business context. The reasoning does not:

Business Requirement → Natural Capability → Configuration → Integration where required → Custom Development only where a real gap remains

That is the reusable part of the approach.

No Custom Code as the Foundation

Standard SAP capabilities should be considered before introducing custom development.

The fact that several SAP capabilities are involved does not automatically mean that a custom layer is required. Sometimes the cleaner architecture is simply to let each standard capability perform the responsibility it already owns.

Technical Implementation: Ground to SAP

The business-first design eventually has to reach the SAP implementation layer.

For evidence, the design can use GOS / Attachment, where supported by the relevant business object or application.

For business attention, Situation Handling can be used according to the applicable scenario and configuration. Manage Situation Types (F2947) is the relevant Fiori application for configuring situation types in supported scenarios.

For physical warehouse movement, the existing EWM process and warehouse tasks remain responsible for execution.

For confirmed warehouse execution history, /SCWM/ORDIM_C is the relevant EWM reference in this design.

The exact configuration path can depend on the SAP release and the specific Situation Handling or EWM scenario. Therefore, technical references should be validated against the actual release and application rather than treated as one universal configuration path.

The technical layer comes after the business requirement has been understood.

Principle 6: Separate Business Requirement From Technical Mechanism

The purpose of this approach is not to reduce the number of SAP components.

It is to avoid making one component responsible for requirements that naturally belong to different capabilities.

The principle is:

Start with the business requirement, identify the SAP capability that naturally owns it, and avoid adding another layer unless the requirement genuinely needs it.

And one question keeps the architecture honest:

"Record of what?"

Core Problem-Solving Pattern: Ground Reality → Exception → WHY → Business Requirement → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation → Business Action

Conclusion

A broken seal may look like a small warehouse exception, but it can expose a much larger architecture problem when every requirement is pushed into one technical mechanism.

The cleaner approach is to separate the requirements.

Let GOS / Attachment handle supporting evidence where appropriate. Let Situation Handling bring the relevant business situation to the responsible user. Let EWM handle the physical warehouse execution. Let EWM execution records provide the warehouse execution history. And let DMS handle genuine document-management requirements when they actually exist.

The objective is not to remove SAP capabilities. The objective is to make each capability responsible for the problem it naturally owns.

Start from the ground. Ask WHY. Identify the real requirement. Then let SAP capabilities do what they are designed to do.

entry.title: The Autonomous Supply Chain is a transformation journey
entry.content:
Executive summary

On Sept 24th, we kicked off our webinar series on SAP Signavio and SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) with the session “The Autonomous Supply Chain Isn’t a Destination — It’s a Transformation Capability.” SAP experts Gunther Sanchez, Timm Hemmert, and Dominik Lehmann shared how supply chain leaders can move from reactive, siloed operations toward a more connected, AI-enabled operating model.

The key message was clear: volatility is now the baseline. Demand uncertainty, trade disruptions, rising costs, and higher customer expectations are putting traditional supply chain models under pressure. AI can help, but the starting point is process transparency — understanding where value is trapped, where bottlenecks occur, and where improvement efforts will have the greatest impact.


Why this matters now

Many supply chain teams still rely on manual work, fragmented systems, and limited end-to-end visibility. This makes it difficult to anticipate issues and often leaves teams firefighting instead of improving performance.

Organizations that invest in process transparency, resilience, and AI-enabled transformation can build a strong competitive advantage. Those that wait risk falling further behind as the gap between reactive and proactive operations grows.

Figure 1: Supply chain leaders face unprecedented challenges — external forces compound internal operational struggles.

What does the Autonomous Supply Chain mean in practice

The autonomous supply chain is not about replacing people. It is about helping people make better, faster decisions with support from AI assistants and agents.

Figure 2: Autonomous SCM helps you deliver on core objectives — from managing uncertainty
to driving efficiency and compliance.

In this model, people continue to set goals, define business rules, approve critical decisions, and manage exceptions. AI supports recurring decisions, monitors process performance, identifies deviations, recommends actions, and executes defined tasks within governed boundaries.

The value comes from connecting signals across planning, inventory, procurement, production, transportation, warehousing, and customer commitments — so teams can move from reactive exception handling to predictive, coordinated operations.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Three high-value opportunity areas

Supply chain transformation leaders often see the greatest potential in three areas.

Figure 3: Three key areas where AI, contextual business data, and end-to-end applications create the most impact.

1. Enhance Planning Performance

Planning teams need to balance inventory, service levels, and cost while dealing with uncertain demand and supply volatility.

SAP Signavio Process Intelligence helps uncover where planning issues originate and why, enabling teams to improve forecast accuracy, reduce stale inventory, and make better cost-service-risk decisions.

2. Optimize Warehouse Operations

Warehouse inefficiencies quickly become customer issues. Bottlenecks in putaway, picking, packing, goods issue posting, and shift execution can increase costs and affect service levels.

By mining SAP EWM processes end to end, SAP Signavio helps teams identify delays, improve throughput, reduce stock-out risks, and lower operating costs.

3. Streamline Transportation Management

Transportation remains one of the most visible and volatile supply chain cost areas.

SAP Signavio Process Intelligence connects to SAP Transportation Management to reveal process deviations, manual interventions, automation gaps, and invoice discrepancies — creating a stronger foundation for data-driven transportation decisions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

From reactive firefighting to proactive process control

A major takeaway from the session was the importance of understanding processes before applying AI. Real-time visibility into open tasks, bottlenecks, and process deviations helps teams act earlier and resolve issues faster.

As Dominik noted: “You should not start with AI. AI should be second. First should be that you really understand how your business processes look, where they are doing well, where they are not doing well.”

Once teams understand the root causes, they can select AI and agent use cases based on value, feasibility, and business priorities.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Real results from real customers

The session highlighted several customer examples showing the impact of process transparency and continuous transformation.

  • Takeda reduced annual supply chain working hours by more than 10% by addressing fragmented global processes and excessive customization.
  • One TCC used SAP Signavio during a rapid SAP S/4HANA transformation, completing ERP implementation from planning to go-live in 67 days.

entry.title: SAP Extended Warehouse Management for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Private Edition, 2025 FPS02 – What’s New
entry.content:
Hello everyone, I hope this article finds you all well. It is once again with great pride and excitement that we would like to announce we have delivered the latest updates for SAP Extended Warehouse Management for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Private Edition, with the 2025 FPS02 release. With this release, we further enhance the Predictive Labor Demand Planning forecasting capabilities by introducing accuracy comparison, add extensibility features for the Advanced Shipping & Receiving integration, deliver business process optimizations and user experience improvements, in the Warehouse Order Streaming, strengthen our Suite Integration capabilities, including new Advanced Returns Management follow-on actions, and much more.

To find out more technical details and information on each feature (such as Customization steps) please review the link the corresponding “What’s New” viewer from the help portal in the title of the subchapters.

And we begin today’s article with a look at the new AI innovations.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Our AI strategy for Logistics and Warehousing is driven by a clear ambition: to help businesses overcome the growing labor and resource challenges in warehouse execution. With this latest release, we continue to build on that vision, reinforcing our long-term strategy and moving another step closer to a smarter, more resilient warehouse operation of the future through intelligent predictive analytics that forecast current and future workloads and through new EWM Agents, which turns insights into executable actions. We enhance everyday warehouse activities with natural language-based interactions with Joule to streamline outbound processes.

Predictive Labor Demand Planning (pLDP) feature enrichment

Building up on the work we have done in the previous releases, with this latest update Predictive Labor Demand Planning (LDP) takes several steps forward, by introducing forecast accuracy evaluation, enhanced APIs support for packing and staging, and a range of user-experience enhancement across the KPI app, monitoring tools, and application logs. A standout addition is the new LDP forecast accuracy KPI card in the FIORI Warehouse KPI app, which uses a 7-day look-back to compare forecasted workload against actual results. Users can drill down by activity area or process step and toggle between absolute and relative deviation views, making it easier to adjust planning and spot trends at a glance.

 On the integration side, the Handling Unit API and the Warehouse Order & Task API now support LDP workload recording for custom-built warehouse confirmation applications. Customers can now leverage the standard labor demand planning features, by enhancing their calling application and providing a start time for the corresponding activity, giving development teams greater flexibility into tailored workflows.

Furthermore, we deliver a new Odata service to support the integration between predictive Labor Demand Planning and the new Warehouse Workload Optimization agent, released in October 2026 for Early Adopter Care program and selected customer groups, as part of SAP’s Logistics Assistant. The agent  will provide the relevant labor demand data to optimize workloads for various resources within the warehouse with accuracy and efficiency.

Please take a look at the collective SAP note 3577311 which collects the released features per feature pack and downport possibilities.

We will shortly release a separate blog post covering the release and functionalities of the new Warehouse Workload Optimization agent, so if you want to find out more about the new optimization capabilities available for SAP EWM, please stay tuned.

Joule: Talk to your warehouse in outbound processes

And that’s not everything we delivered in terms of AI functionalities with this release. Joule can now converse directly with warehouse users to streamline outbound processes through natural language. Whether you need to create, cancel, or confirm warehouse tasks, set or reverse the "Ready for Shipping" status, or post and cancel goods issues, Joule handles it all through a simple conversation, guiding users through multiple screens to get things done. Beyond executing actions, Joule also acts as a troubleshooting partner, helping users investigate blocking reasons on EWM Outbound Delivery Orders (ODOs) and guiding them toward quick resolutions. It’s a smarter, more intuitive way to keep your warehouse moving.

ADVANCED SHIPPING & RECEIVING

Integration between transportation and warehouse logistics is a significant contributor towards logistics efficiency, synchronizing process changes between warehouse and transportation, reducing overall logistics-costs by optimizing and streamlining freight planning with warehouse execution. To further tighten this integration, with this release we provide the following enhancements options.

  • Enhancement concept for product hierarchy integration – we have expanded advanced shipping and receiving with support for the Kit-to-Order (KTO) process, unlocking greater flexibility for outbound operations. This release enables KTO across multiple process variants, including warehouse-driven ODO split, transportation-driven ODO split, and late transportation-driven ODO split (triggered at loading completion), all designed with one clear goal in mind: keeping item hierarchies consistent throughout the end-to-end process. It’s worth noting that nested BOM hierarchies and inbound processes are currently out of scope. This enhancement options is fully supported for both embedded and decentral ASR deployments, giving you the flexibility to adopt it in the setup that best fits your landscape.

  • New SAP Global Trade Services (GTS) integration BAdI – we introduced a new Business Add-in (BAdI) for SAP Global Trade Services (GTS) integration, giving customers even greater flexibility when it comes to compliance checks in outbound processes. Through the existing BAdI /SCWM/EX_GTS_PARAMETERS, additional products, such as components of finished articles that aren’t part of the EWM Outbound Delivery Order, can now be included in the GTS compliance check. Complementing this, the newly introduced BAdI /SCWM/EX_GTS_CHECK_RESULT allows the compliance check results for those additional product items to be evaluated and the aggregated check result to be influenced. To keep the integration compliant, results can only be adjusted following a conservative strategy, meaning an "OK" result can be changed to "NOT OK", but not the other way around. As with our other enhancements, this feature is supported for both embedded and decentral ASR scenarios.

CONTINUOUS MODERNIZATION & SIMPLIFICATION

Our commitment to modernization and continuous improvements not only enhances functionality but also provides users with a seamless and intuitive interaction, helping businesses drive efficiency, optimize processes, and deliver superior experiences to their stakeholders. To that end, I would like to highlight the following features from this latest release.

Warehouse order streaming – pick path optimization

One of the biggest and exciting highlights of this release is the introduction of warehouse order streaming, also called the ‘Pick-Path Optimization’ for SAP Extended Warehouse Management. This powerful new capability, which is directly embedded in EWM, is designed to make order picking faster and smarter, particularly in e-commerce and retail scenarios where pick-card based picking of small orders is common. With this feature, EWM Warehouse Orders can be flexibly created or re-bundled based on local EWM optimization algorithms that take both the optimal pick path and the resource (type) layout into account, helping pickers move through the warehouse more efficiently and reducing unnecessary travel time.

The pick-path optimization supports different key process steps, including System-Guided RF Picking and/or Wave Release, and can be activated and configured flexibly per queue, activity area, and warehouse order creation rule to match your operational needs. To help you find the best setup, the feature also supports simulation and algorithm comparison, with results visualized directly through the EWM Graphic Warehouse Layout (GWL), making it easy to evaluate different strategies before rolling them out on the floor.

Renovation in Segmentation processes with EWM

We’re excited to introduce several comprehensive enhancements in EWM Segmentation, making it easier than ever to work with segmented stock across your warehouse processes. Previously, using segmentation required a dedicated characteristic in the batch master but with this release, that requirement is gone. For batch-managed products and articles, there’s no longer a need to enhance batch characteristics just to use segmentation, simplifying setup and reducing maintenance overhead. The new capability also allows the validation of the stock segment to be skipped when it meets your business needs.

To put this into context: while batch classification describes stock and its detailed properties (like expiration date, production date, or country of origin) without being limited to predefined values, stock segmentation offers a logical or commercial division of stock using predefined values, helping to improve planning, forecasting, and material distribution.

With this release, segmentation is supported across a broad range of processes, including inbound processing (with GR Preparation and RF Receiving), putaway with exception handling, outbound processing, ad-hoc warehouse tasks and movements, picking with exception handling, posting changes, staging for and receiving from production, MES-driven staging, physical inventory, Goods Receipt Preparation (GRPI) for production, stock migration via the Migration Cockpit, initial stock upload (via /SCWM/ISU), and the planned customer return process, giving consistent, end-to-end segmentation support wherever it matters. We have also created a collective SAP note 3734726 which contains all details including corrective notes, and customers can select to implement based on their business processes.

Other modernization and optimization enhancements

Aside from the highlights mentioned above, here is a quick rundown of some more optimization and modernization enhancements delivered with this release:

  • Close HU in RF Packing Transaction – we have enhanced the Radio Frequency (RF) Packing transaction. Now users can close Handling Unit packing steps (process-oriented storage control) directly from the RF packing transaction without having to navigate to a separate transaction.
  • ERP Integration for Migration Cockpit – we enabled stock updates in ERP to happen directly during migration. This enhancement is particularly interesting for customers who run both – ERP (e.g. greenfield) and EWM (e.g. migration) transformation projects in parallel. To make this possible, a new EWM setting has been introduced that activates ERP integration for stock migration, giving you full control over when and how it’s applied. Best of all, the feature is supported for both migration approaches — staging tables and direct transfer — ensuring a smoother, more consistent migration experience regardless of the path you choose.
  • International Organization for Standardization (ISO) unit of measure support for WCU IDocs – with this feature, you can use units of measure supported by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in Warehouse Control Unit (WCU) IDoc communication. Using ISO-compliant units of measure contributes to standardized communication of quantities across SAP and external systems, reducing mapping efforts, and improving reliability of warehouse task processing across system boundaries. This feature adds new versions of the IDoc for sending and receiving WTs to a non-SAP system (IDoc /SCWM/WMTOID01) and the IDoc for confirming warehouse tasks (IDoc /SCWM/WMTCID01) that include fields for ISO-compliant units of measure in addition to the existing internal units of measure.

  • New Warehouse Monitor node to monitor PPF actions – with this release we have also made it easier to monitor and manage Post Processing Framework (PPF) actions via the EWM Warehouse Monitor. You can now select and work with PPF actions directly from the monitor, using the dedicated PPF Actions node to search for actions that have been successfully processed, failed, or are still pending execution. Users can look across multiple PPF applications and apply PPF-specific selection criteria to zero in on exactly what is needed. Once you’ve made your selection, the system gives you a clear view of each action’s processing status, PPF application, action definition, and other relevant details. For actions that have already been processed, you can dive into the processing log to investigate further. And to help you work more efficiently, a new monitor method called Process lets you execute up to 50 PPF actions at a time, turning what used to be a repetitive task into a quick, streamlined action.

SUITE INTEGRATION

Integration is a core pillar of our investments, by which we provide a deep and native integration with SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud solution components, along with other SAP cloud solution offerings for seamless integration of comprehensive logistics end-to-end processes incl. production integration, customs processing and more. With SAP S/4HANA Cloud, private edition 2025, FPS2 we deliver the following enhancements.

Advanced Returns Management (ARM) follow-up action to refurbish using Production Order/Maintenance Order

With this release we introduce two new logistics follow-on actions for Advanced Returns Management (ARM): Refurbishment using Maintenance Order (0036) and Refurbishment using Production Order (0037). When a returned and one of the two new follow-up actions is selected, a new Initiator process code (ARF) per follow-up action kicks in, triggering either an EWM Posting Change or an Outbound Delivery Order to set the refurbishment process in motion. The decision to refurbish can be made early on by a sales representative at returns order creation, or later by a receiving clerk during material inspection — giving teams flexibility at every stage. The solution supports a range of scenarios, whether you’re working with EWM-managed or IM-managed storage locations, and handles the full flow from receiving and inspection through to refurbishment. To keep things traceable, the Inspection Reference is stored as a stock attribute for unique identification, and the feature works seamlessly across both embedded and decentral EWM deployments.

Partial Goods Issue for Batch-Managed Component Consumption in Manufacturing

One other enhancement for the topic of production integration worth highlighting is the informational gap that occurs sometimes between the physical reality on the shop floor and what's reflected in the system.

As an example, let us assume there are 10 pieces of Batch A physically sitting in the Production Supply Area (PSA), but the system only shows 6. This can occur because the warehouse task that moved the other 4 pieces hasn't been confirmed yet, even if the components were already delivered. So, when the production worker goes to record the consumption, they enter all 10 pieces that were used. The system can only post a goods issue for the 6 pieces it knows about, and the remaining 4 end up flagged in the Reprocess Goods Movements app (COGI) for follow-up. With this new enhancement, we can better support these exceptional situations.

When it comes to batch-managed components, the system applies different quantity split variants depending on how your process is set up. If you use batch determination and haven’t specified a component batch in your manufacturing order, the system posts the available quantity and automatically creates a postprocessing record for the missing amount. You can then handle the remainder using the Reprocess Goods Movements app (transaction COGI) and in this scenario, the Goods Issue Quantity Split checkbox in your production scheduling profile doesn’t come into play.

On the other hand, if you’re not using batch determination and enter the batch number during production confirmation, the Goods Issue Quantity Split checkbox becomes relevant and controls how the split is handled. The same applies when you specify a component batch directly in the manufacturing order. The batch determination isn’t needed in that case, but the checkbox does take effect.

Quality Management integration feature enrichments

Finally, when it comes to Suite integration, as with every release, we further deepened the capabilities of Quality Management integration via the following updates:

  • Enhancement for container-based sample size calculation – we introduced the capability to automatically derive the number and type of containers during inspection lot creation, whether that happens at goods receipt or during early warehouse task creation. This enhancement is supported in ‘IOT4 – Q-Inspection Product/Batch Inbound Delivery’, helping quality teams save time and improve consistency right from the start of the inbound process. To give full flexibility, a new customizing option lets you define the container count mode for both packed and unpacked scenarios. For packed stock, the count can be derived from handling units — either at the highest or lowest level — while for unpacked stock, the system can use stock-specific units of measure (SUoM) or a packaging specification to determine the count. And for teams with unique requirements, a new BAdI (/SCWM/EX_QM_CONT_COUNT_DETN) in enhancement spot /SCWM/ES_QM_INSP is available for custom implementations. The feature is supported for both embedded and decentral EWM deployments, with the restriction that the QM component is in SAP S/4HANA 2022 or later. 
  • Prevent partial usage decision in case of missing required quality certificate – for products that require a quality certificate, we introduced a safeguard to ensure that a partial usage decision can now only be made once the receipt of the quality certificate has been confirmed. During EWM partial usage decision processing, the system checks against the Inspection Lot certificate status "CTCM – Certificate Missing", preventing premature decisions when documentation isn’t yet in place. To give full control, a new customizing option allows the certificate check to be enabled per EWM Inspection Object Type (IOT), so you can tailor the behavior to fit your specific quality processes. The feature is supported for both embedded EWM deployments (including synchronous goods receipt) and decentral EWM deployments.

CLEAN CORE & EXTENSIBILITY

The Clean Core Extensibility strategy aims to provide a modern and powerful integration option and to enable efficient upgrade projects for customers and partners. Alongside supporting this strategy, we continuously adapt solution content to modernize and simplify the user experience. By regularly updating and refining Extended Warehouse Management for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, private edition, we ensure we remain relevant and effective in meeting current needs.

In the SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS02 release we continue to deliver on this with the following highlights:

  • New Odata Service for Wave header & items – we delivered the A2X ODATA service on wave header and items with various read and change actions:
    • Get Wave header & item details
    • Get Warehouse orders by wave
    • Assign, unassign WMR items to wave
    • Lock, unlock, merge, split wave
    • Release wave and get wave release log
    • Simulate wave release and get simulation log
  • Enhance Odata Service for warehouse resource – we also enhanced the existing ODATA-service for Warehouse Resource to support the action of assigning & unassigning resources to resource groups

FIND OUT MORE!

To see more details on the above-mentioned topics as well as see what other enhancements we delivered with this release I highly encourage you to explore our latest “SAP Extended Warehouse Management for SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2025, Private Edition, FPS02” slide deck.

You can also find more technical details and documentation on the above listed topic and others we left out via the “What’s New” viewer on the Help Documentation portal.

entry.title: SAP EWM - Change WPT During Delivery Creation using BADI
entry.content:
Introduction

In many retail and distribution businesses, a customer order is created with a single shipping location, but the goods must be delivered to multiple store locations. Although the sales order and outbound delivery are created from a common shipping point, warehouse execution requires store-specific picking logic.

A recent business requirement involved ensuring that:

  • One Sales Order contains multiple Store Locations.
  • During EWM Outbound Delivery Order (ODO) creation, the Warehouse Process Type (WPT) must be determined based on the Store Location.
  • Warehouse Tasks (WTs) belonging to the same store should be assigned to the same warehouse operator.
  • Multiple WTs should be combined into a single Warehouse Order (WO) through Warehouse Order Creation Rules (WOCR).
  • Standard WPT determination was insufficient because store information was not part of the standard determination criteria.

To address this requirement, a custom enhancement was implemented using BADI /SCWM/EX_DLV_DET_PROCTYPE, method CHANGE_PROCTYPE, which SAP provides for modifying the Warehouse Process Type determined during delivery processing. The BADI can be used to change the warehouse process type after SAP's standard determination logic has executed.

Business Scenario

Existing Process

  1. Sales Order is created in SAP S/4HANA.
  2. Outbound Delivery is generated.
  3. Delivery is distributed to SAP EWM.
  4. EWM creates the Outbound Delivery Order (ODO).
  5. Standard WPT determination occurs.
  6. Warehouse Tasks are created.

Challenge

The shipment contains materials destined for different store locations.

Example:

Using the same WPT for all items results in:

  • Warehouse Tasks being split across different WOCR strategies.
  • Multiple Warehouse Orders being created.
  • Different users receiving tasks for the same shipment.
  • Reduced warehouse productivity and increased travel distance.

The business required store-specific WPT determination so that downstream WOCR logic could consolidate Warehouse Tasks into a single executable Warehouse Order.

Solution Design

Enhancement Point

SAP EWM provides BAdI:

/SCWM/EX_DLV_DET_PROCTYPE

Purpose:

  • Replace standard WPT determination.
  • Adjust the Warehouse Process Type after standard determination.
  • Apply customer-specific determination logic during delivery creation or modification.

Conclusion

When a business requires a single sales order and shipping location to serve multiple store destinations, standard Warehouse Process Type determination may not be sufficient. By implementing BAdI /SCWM/EX_DLV_DET_PROCTYPE using method CHANGE_PROCTYPE, it is possible to dynamically assign store-specific Warehouse Process Types during EWM ODO creation. SAP documentation explicitly states that this BAdI can be used to change the warehouse process type determined by the standard system.

entry.title: The Extended Warehouse Management in SAP S/4HANA FAQ Series: Joule skills in SAP EWM
entry.content:
As many of our EWM customers are excited to learn what AI Joule capabilities are coming in the next releases with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition for EWM, we’ve decided to write this blog to share a little bit of an overview of what newly released features are already available and how customers can get access to them.

What is SAP Joule, and where can I get the latest information on Joule?
We update constantly the official documentation of SAP Joule, and you can always refer to the official documentation here.

What are the different types of skills that Joule is capable of?
In general, there are different interaction patterns that are offered by Joule capabilities:

  • Informational. Joule can understand your questions with human natural languages and provide relevant context regarding the queried SAP business objects.
  • Navigational. Users can ask Joule to help navigate and open the correct FIORI apps and SAP transactions to perform certain business processes.
  • Transactional. Joule can understand the questions and retrieve the necessary business data from the backend SAP system and react on the user instructions to trigger executable steps directly in the backend systems.
  • Analytical. Joule can provide real time analytical views on certain business processes and steps within SAP systems.

In the following paragraphs, we provide a breakdown of each Joule skill.

Joule informational skills in EWM
As part of the centrally delivered Joule skills, it understands automatically also the EWM context and business objects based on trained SAP help documentation. EWM customers can ask any relevant questions, and Joule will be able to search for the data and provide a summary as well as trusted link to the SAP help documentation. The following screenshots provide a simple example on the Joule documentation flow:

 

 Joule navigational skills in SAP EWM
We have enabled EWM navigational Joule skills with some of our frequently-used EWM FIORI apps and SAP GUI for HTML transactions as of 2509 release.

This is particularly useful when we have new users that would like to familiarize themselves with EWM transactions and find the most suitable transactions to perform certain EWM processes. For a list of full Joule EWM navigation capabilities, refer to this SAP Note 3523238, or the official SAP help documentation.

The following screen shots provide an example of EWM Joule navigation flow, where the user would like to create product warehouse tasks:

 

 Note: the default warehouse setting on FIORI also plays a role here, that by navigating to the FIORI app.

Joule transactional skills in EWM – Talk to your warehouse Outbound process
Our first Joule scenario focuses on the Warehouse Outbound process, where the users can get all details of outbound delivery orders (ODOs) on the header and item level. The Joule skills are released according to monthly Joule release calendar in the following phases:

  • 2511 release: read outbound delivery order and item
  • 2512 release: query outbound delivery order and item
  • 2602 release: read warehouse order and tasks, read ODO properties
